#7624. Wise Words from Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas as to Access to Court Records

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

My Stanford law school colleagues Nora and David Engstrom, as well as Berkeley law professor Jonah Gelbach and others, have asked the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules recommend a new Rule of Civil Procedure (5.3) governing the sealing of court records. I think this is an excellent idea: While there is a good deal of precedent on the question, distilling it into a rule that can easily be consulted by judges, lawyers, law clerks, and pro se litigants would be very helpful.

Just today, Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas (also a former law professor), submitted a letter endorsing the proposed rule, and I thought it was much worth passing along:

Dear Members of the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules:

I write to express my strong support for proposed Rule 5.3, a much-needed recapitulation of the procedural standards governing sealing of judicial records.

The public has a presumptive right to access judicial records. This right serves several important societal functions. By exposing the records of private wrongdoing to the public eye, this right deters further wrongdoing. By forcing the government to litigate out in the open, it empowers the public "to keep a watchful eye on the workings of public agencies." Nixon v. Warner Commc'ns, Inc., 435 U.S. 589, 598 (1978). And by enabling the public to dig into the bases for judicial decisions, it enables the public to assure itself of the strength of judicial reasoning, the cornerstone of judicial legitimacy. This right thus not only "diminishes possibilities for injustice, incompetence, perjury, and fraud," but also provides "the public with a more complete understanding of the judicial system and a better perception of its fairness." In re Avandia Mktg., Sales Prac. & Prod. Liab. Litig., 924 F.3d 662, 672 (3d Cir. 2019) (internal quotation marks omitted).

On paper, this right looks strong. In the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, where I sit, a district court issuing an order to seal "must articulate the compelling, countervailing interests to be protected" and "make specific findings on the record concerning the effects of disclosure." Id. (internal quotation marks omitted). But that standard is a paper tiger—mighty in appearance, but toothless in practice. Time and again, we see cases on appeal where the parties asked to seal large parts of the record below, and the district court, with little discussion, agreed to do so.

Take one recent motion to seal in a Third Circuit case. The district court had certified a multi-state class action against a car company. On appeal, the company asked us to seal ten volumes of appendices, totaling nearly three thousand pages of material. The company told us that sealing was necessary to prevent competitors from copying its design choices, stealing its engineering solutions, and exploiting its sales strategy.

But it took only a cursory glance at the appendices to see how overbroad the company's request was. Hundreds of pages, for example, covered deposition testimony from one of the plaintiff's lay witnesses, a mechanic who had worked on the defendant's cars and had commented on their alleged defects. Hundreds of other pages dealt with one of the plaintiffs' experts, who had opined on the veracity of the defendant's public comments and sales catalogues. But if the mechanic based his testimony on his day-to-day work on the defendant's cars, and the expert had based his testimony on the company's public statements, how would these materials reveal competitive secrets? So I denied the request without prejudice, asking the company to come back with a narrower request if it so chose. But why had the record below been sealed in the first place?

It should come as little surprise that motions to seal almost always go unopposed. The harm of overbroad sealing falls on future victims of repeat tortfeasors, future litigants in related cases, and the public at large. It does not fall on the parties to the case.

Indeed, the parties generally have an active interest in secrecy. The party who moves to seal records fears that the information produced in the case could lead to bad press coverage, competitive harms, or even follow-on litigation. The other party presumably does not share those same concerns about broad disclosure, but it does not share the public's concerns about overbroad sealing, either.

So in the give-and-take game of litigation, where it can be important to reserve your capital for fighting the fights that matter to your client, opposing a motion to seal is a waste of that capital. At the very least, it is a waste of time and money. For lawyers in an active dispute—so used to viewing themselves as only agents of their clients, and not also officers of the court—submitting an opposition to an overbroad motion to seal might not seem worth the cost of the paper to print it.

This leaves it to district-court judges to police these motions and protect the public's presumptive right of access to judicial records. But what my experience as a judge on the court of appeals has taught me, Professor Engstrom et. al's empirical work now confirms: Most district courts rubber-stamp these requests.

This might come as a surprise to some members of the Judicial Conference. After all, the law of every circuit requires district courts to reject requests to seal that are too broad to be justified by their supposed rationale.

So why do district courts frequently fail to apply that law? One problem might be the lack of developed precedent in this area. Because motions to seal are almost never subject to full treatment in district court opinions, let alone appellate review, there are few decisions applying legal standards to specific facts, teasing out what interests suffice to justify sealing, and how broad is too broad. Without clearly factually analogous precedent to rely on, district courts might be more hesitant to deny a motion to seal as overbroad, even though the operative legal standard compels that result.

Another problem is rooted in the lack of adversarial presentation. With no one on the other side, inflated claims of confidentiality go unchallenged.

Other problems might boil down to the mechanics of busy district court dockets. Perhaps, for example, when a district court grants a protective order, that decision generates an inertial force that skews the outcome of the subsequent motion to seal, even though the two decisions are subject to different legal standards. Or perhaps a motion to seal, because it is unopposed, slips under the radar, resembling an administrative matter to be rubber-stamped rather than a legal decision to be carefully scrutinized.

But whatever the reason, the results are clear: For most motions to seal, "the parties agree, the busy district court accommodates, and nobody is left in the courtroom to question whether the decision satisfied the substantive requirements." Binh Hoa Le v. Exeter Fin. Corp., 990 F.3d 410, 417 (5th Cir. 2021).

This proposed rule will push parties and courts alike to do better. First, this proposed rule will ensure that the parties know what their obligations are when they submit a motion to seal. I often sit by designation on the District of Delaware, where I regularly receive motions to seal with no accompanying explanation or justification, putting the onus on me to push the parties for more. Under Proposed Rule 5.3(c), parties will be reminded that, as our circuit has regularly held, "[b]road allegations of harm, bereft of specific examples or articulated reasoning, are insufficient." In re Avandia Mktg., 924 F.3d at 673 (internal quotation marks omitted).

Second, this proposed rule will act as a process-forcing mechanism for busy district court judges. District courts lack the benefit of adversarial litigation over motions to seal. And without a party opposing a motion, it is easy to think that no reasoning is needed for an order—if no party loses, the thinking goes, no party needs a basis for the court's decision.

Proposed Rule 5.3(h) makes clear that even without an adversarial party, the district court must act as the steward of the public interest in accessing court records, and must reason through its decision. The decision to seal is for the court to make by applying the correct legal standard, not for the parties to make by means of consent. Proposed Rule 5.3(i) provides a checklist that a district court can use in reaching that decision.

Finally, the proposed rule will remind parties and district courts alike that sealing is not an all-or-nothing question. Proposed Rule 5.3(d)(3) and (g) make clear that, where viable, the default approach should be targeted redactions. The choice is not between disclosing a list of social security numbers and sealing an entire document. A happy medium is often readily available.

This proposed rule does not make new law. Sunlight is the best disinfectant for many societal ills, yet sealing "insulates the participants" in the legal process, "masking impropriety, obscuring incompetence, and concealing corruption." Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. v. F.T.C., 710 F.2d 1165, 1179 (6th Cir. 1983). Judicial reasoning is the basis for judicial legitimacy, yet sealing "withdraws an element of the judicial process from public view," making "the ensuing decision look more like fiat." Matter of Krynicki, 983 F.2d 74, 75 (7th Cir. 1992) (Easterbrook, J.). For these reasons, the courts of appeals have consistently held that the public has a presumptive right to access judicial records, one that should only be abrogated where necessary, and even there only to the extent necessary. This proposed rule simply makes that right harder to neglect.

My then-student Jennifer Welson and I had unsuccessfully proposed a sealing rule to the Rule Committee in 2020, on behalf of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and Electronic Frontier Foundation; but I much hope that the Engstrom et al. proposal, which is backed by considerably more empirical research than mine had been, will be more successful.

#7621. Op-Ed: Crime Drops—Locally Collected Data Drives National Headlines

A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Share on X X.com Share on Facebook Facebook Email Email

This opinion piece by CJIS Special Agent in Charge Timothy A. Ferguson was published by the Bridgeport News on October 19, 2026.

Across the country, you saw the headlines. Violent crime declined historically last year—dropping an estimated 9.3% from 2024 to 2025. Murder and nonnegligent manslaughter estimated offenses saw an even larger dip of 18.1%.

In West Virginia, crime was also trending downward.

These headlines are based on data reported to the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program by more than 17,000 agencies, covering 96.2% of the U.S. population. It is the responsibility of the FBI’s UCR Program, located within the Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Division, in Clarksburg, West Virginia, to collect and publish the data from all 50 states to provide a national picture of reported crime.

This is no small feat. Every day, states and agencies translate local and state crime categories into the national standard and submit their data to the FBI. The UCR Program publishes this data monthly on the Crime Data Explorer to promote transparency and allow you to view timely crime data.

The program also uses the data to develop special reports on topics that matter to you — such as crime in schools, aggravated assault with a firearm, and teen/domestic violence. Then once a year, the program sorts through more than 700 million data points to present you the annual snapshot of crime.

Data collection is just a small fraction of what is accomplished at the CJIS Division. Other efforts also make headlines or prevent you from seeing a tragedy on the news.

Tips actioned by the National Threat Operations Center (NTOC) stop school shootings and help with investigations. Super intelligence capabilities incorporated into NTOC enhance the speed and precision of tip triage, strengthening our ability to process the highest priority tips first so we can promptly share critical threat information with federal, state, and local law enforcement.

Criminal history information from the Interstate Identification Index prevents criminals from becoming your child’s teacher or bus driver. Wants and warrants within the National Crime Information Center help police arrest violent criminals.

Detectives can identify subjects and victims through fingerprints submitted to the Next Generation Identification System.

The division’s mission is to provide our partners with the criminal justice information they need while preserving civil liberties. Sharing that information with officers on the frontlines results in arrests that take criminals off the street and keep neighborhoods safe.

It helps law enforcement return to their families at the end of their shifts. It crushes violent crime and defends the homeland.

When you see headlines of declining crime, know the work to determine that, and the investigations that preceded it, are touched by your neighbors dedicated to the mission at the FBI’s CJIS Division.

Timothy A. Ferguson is assistant director in charge of the FBI’s Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Division in Clarksburg, West Virginia. CJIS provides vital systems and services to local, state, tribal, and federal agencies that help ensure public safety. These include the National Crime Information Center; the FBI’s Next Generation Identification System and associated biometric services; the National Instant Criminal Background Check System for firearm purchases; the National Threat Operations Center, which receives and processes tips from the public; and the Uniform Crime Reporting Program, which publishes crime and law enforcement statistical data.

#7619. Fifth Circuit on Pseudonymity of Libel Defendant (Who Claims She Was Sexually Assaulted)

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Doe v. Roe, decided today by Fifth Circuit Judges Jennifer Walker Elrod, Carolyn Dineen King, and Carl Stewart:

After receiving notice of Jane Roe's impending California lawsuit involving allegations of sexual assault and sexual harassment, John Doe sued Roe in the Southern District of Mississippi, alleging that Roe was attempting to extort and defame him. Roe moved to proceed pseudonymously in the Mississippi lawsuit. The district court denied her permission to do so. Roe appeals that decision, raising several concerns with the district court's analysis. Because we agree with some of Roe's arguments, we vacate and remand for the district court to reconsider whether Roe should be allowed to proceed pseudonymously….

Roe argues that allegations of sexual assault involve matters of the utmost intimacy [and can thus justify pseudonymity]. We agree. There is no doubt that requiring alleged rape and sexual assault victims to proceed "under their real identities would require them to disclose information of the utmost intimacy." It is no surprise, then, that numerous courts have allowed alleged victims of sexual misconduct to proceed under a pseudonym, "including when they are defendants being sued for libel and related torts."

We agree with Roe. To start, we are not persuaded that the proverbial cat is out of the bag here. True, publicly available information cannot be obscured by courts. However, that internet sleuths might speculate that Roe is a particular person because her California complaint "lines up with [her] public profile" is not the same as a public broadcasting of Roe's certain identity. As to the fact that Roe's name was a matter of public record for short periods, that was either because of Doe's actions (which Roe objected to), or Roe's inadvertent disclosures which counsel corrected and constituted no waiver (which we address below)….

Last, Roe argues that she did not waive her right to proceed anonymously. Again, we agree. Roe never waived her ability to request pseudonymity because her conduct does not constitute an "intentional relinquishment" of that position. Roe's opposition to Doe's motion to proceed pseudonymously waived nothing because Roe's position was that she should be allowed to proceed pseudonymously while he should not be. And any confusion about Roe's position based on the precise language in her opposition brief was clarified by her own subsequent motions seeking to seal or redact Doe's amended complaint (which used Roe's real name) and to proceed pseudonymously.

Further, Doe's use of Roe's real name in open court did not constitute waiver on Roe's behalf because, at the time, Doe had already publicly named Roe in his amended complaint, Roe had a pending motion seeking to seal or redact that amended complaint naming her, and Roe objected to the use of her name at the hearing (even if not as fast as a prudent attorney likely should have). Finally, we are not convinced that Roe's inadvertent disclosures of her real name in the California case and on this appeal constitute waiver. The disclosures were unintentional, were made in portions of larger filings, and Roe took steps to correct the errors once becoming aware of them, resulting in the sealing and refiling of the documents. These facts do not demonstrate that Roe intentionally relinquished her request to proceed pseudonymously….

In light of the clarifications provided in this opinion, we find that it is appropriate to allow the district court to reconsider whether Roe should be permitted to proceed under a pseudonym in this case. {We acknowledge Doe's argument that allowing Roe to proceed under a pseudonym would be prejudicial to him. We think that argument is best left for the district court to address in the first instance on remand.}

Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, of Ontario, Canada, was sentenced today to 50 years in prison for offenses related to a 2020 attack on correctional officers at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood. This sentence will run consecutive to the 40-year sentence he is currently serving for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS.

“Bahnasawy, who is already serving a 40-year sentence in federal prison for plotting mass casualty attacks in New York City on behalf of ISIS, savagely attacked corrections officers once again on behalf of ISIS,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time.”

“We will prosecute those who aid, attempt to aid, or commit violence on behalf of the pernicious ISIS ideology wherever they may be found,” said U.S. Attorney Brian D. Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania. “Today’s sentence reflects our unwavering commitment to fight those who perpetrate violence in the name of ISIS even behind prison walls.”

“Although he was behind bars, this convicted terrorist committed a horrific attack on two corrections officers in the name of ISIS, which they fortunately survived,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “Today’s sentencing shows that violent attacks by those who support the evil ideology of ISIS or other foreign terrorist organizations cannot be tolerated by our society. Fighting terrorism is a central part of the FBI’s mission to protect the American people, and the FBI is committed to working with our law enforcement partners to hold these vicious criminals accountable.”

Bahnasawy was an inmate at USP Allenwood who, on Dec. 7, 2020, attacked two corrections officers using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell. Bahnasawy stabbed one officer in the head and face, and, when a second responded to assist, Bahnasawy stabbed her in the hand.

The first officer eventually lost his right eye as a result of the attack. When Bahnasawy was restrained, a note was found in his sock that read, “This is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.” A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) was also found taped to the inside of a locker door in Bahnasawy’s prison cell. Bahnasawy pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to ISIS, a designated foreign terrorist organization.

At the time of the attacks at USP Allenwood, Bahnasawy was serving a 40-year sentence for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS. Bahnasawy, a then-20-year-old Canadian citizen and resident, plotted with Talha Haroon and Russell Salic to conduct bombings and shootings in heavily populated areas of New York City during the Islamic holy month of Ramadhan in 2016, all in the name of ISIS.

An undercover FBI agent (UC) infiltrated the co-conspirators’ terrorist plot, posing as an ISIS supporter prepared to join in the attacks. The FBI arrested Bahnasawy in May 2016 after he traveled from Canada to the New York City area in preparation for the attacks, and he has been in custody since that time.

This case was investigated by the FBI’s Philadelphia Field Office.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Geoffrey MacArthur for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and Deputy Chief Larry Schneider of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section prosecuted the case.

#7613. No Problem with Recognizing Islamic Talaq Divorce from Dubai, When Wife Didn't Want to Stay Married

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Schultz v. Stevenson, decided today by California Court of Appeal Judges Peter Krause, Shama Hakim Mesiwala, and Stacy Boulware Eurie:

In 2004, [the parties] purchased a residential property in Grass Valley, California, taking title as "husband and wife as joint tenants." In 2020, [husband] Schultz obtained a judgment of divorce from [wife] Stevenson in Dubai, United Arab Emirates (UAE). The Dubai divorce decree addressed marital status and child custody only; it made no findings related to division of property or spousal support.

Years later, Schultz commenced an action … to partition the Grass Valley property [by ordering it sold and the proceeds split -EV]. Stevenson opposed partition, arguing that the Dubai divorce decree is not enforceable in California and therefore the property is community property and not subject to partition [since California law does not allow partition of community property among married parties -EV]. The trial court ultimately … [decided] in favor of Schultz, finding that the parties are divorced and that the property is not community property….

Stevenson … argues that the trial court abused its discretion by extending comity to the Dubai divorce decree because it was based on Islamic (Sharia) laws that violate state public policy and constitutional principles of equal protection and due process…. [S]he argues that the Dubai divorce is not entitled to comity because it is based on a talaq pronouncement of divorce, which violates California's public policy favoring gender equality and constitutional protections against gender-based disparate treatment. [Generally, a talaq divorce can only be initiated by a husband. -EV] Stevenson contends therefore that she and Schultz are still married, and that the Nevada County property is community property, which is not subject to partition.

We conclude that Stevenson has failed to show that the trial court erred in extending comity to the Dubai divorce decree.

Under the doctrine of comity, courts of this nation generally will give effect to the judgment of a foreign nation if the foreign court had proper jurisdiction and enforcement of the judgment will not prejudice the rights of United States citizens or violate domestic public policy…. Even if we agree that parts of Sharia law—such as a talaq pronouncement of divorce—are contrary to domestic public policy favoring gender equality and constitutional protections against gender-based disparate treatment, the mere fact that some laws of the foreign nation are inconsistent with those of the sovereign does not preclude application of comity.

The basic principle of judicial comity is that "'a court should not assume to disturb another court's disposition of a controversy unless there are good reasons for doing so.'" The standard for refusing to enforce a foreign judgment on public policy grounds is high and infrequently met. The standard "'is not simply that the law is contrary to our public policy, but that it is so offensive to our public policy as to be "'prejudicial to recognized standards of morality and to the general interests of the citizens….'"' [E]ven when a foreign law offends public policy, 'it may still be applied in a limited context where the potential harm is minimal….'" (See In re Dalip Singh Bir's Estate (Cal. App. 1948) [in context of intestate succession, foreign law permitting polygamy may be applied under principles of comity].)

Here, we are not persuaded that extending comity to the Dubai divorce decree impermissibly prejudiced Stevenson's rights or flouted state public policy favoring gender equality. It is important to remember that the Dubai judgment only adjudicated two issues—marital status and child custody—and that the trial court extended comity to the judgment as it related to the status of marriage only. {Stevenson contends that issues related to child custody and support have been rendered moot as the children have reached the age of majority.} Since Stevenson plainly did not wish to remain married to Schultz, we cannot say that it was an abuse of discretion for the trial court to recognize the Dubai judgment as dissolving marital status.

The premise underlying Stevenson's claim of prejudice appears to be that recognizing the foreign divorce precludes her from obtaining spousal support and an equitable division of the marital property. We disagree with this premise…. As noted, the Dubai judgment only adjudicated the issues of marital status and child custody. It did not address, and therefore has no effect upon, spousal support or the division of community property in California….

In reaching this conclusion, we note that the trial court has ordered the partition and sale of property but has not yet determined how the proceeds will be disbursed, reserving jurisdiction "to order the manner in which the sale proceeds are to be disbursed, and to order equitable adjustments that the Court considers just and appropriate." It is therefore premature for us to consider whether the distribution of proceeds amounts to an abuse of discretion….

Robin D. Shofner (Scale LLP) represents Schultz.

#7612. Canadian law firms see increased cyberattacks, data breaches

Four Canadian law firms have said they experienced recent data breaches amid concerns that cyberattacks are increasingly targeting the legal and financial industries. (Image from Shutterstock)

Four Canadian law firms have said they experienced recent data breaches amid concerns that cyberattacks are increasingly targeting the legal and financial industries.

McCarthy Tétrault, Borden Ladner Gervais, Bennett Jones and Davies Ward Phillips & Vineberg said the damage has been contained and that they are alerting clients affected by the breaches. The federal Canadian Centre for Cyber Security issued a warning last week about an ongoing phishing campaign targeting organizations in the legal and financial sectors.

“Multiple Canadian firms have been targeted by individuals impersonating internal IT support and directing employees to fraudulent sign-in pages,” according to the warning.

#7611. Don't Expect a Lame-Duck Supreme Court Vacancy (But There Are Other Nominations to Consider)

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Both the NYT and Bloomberg reports that Justice Alito still intends to finish out the current Supreme Court term.

There has been rampant speculation that one of the older conservative justices (namely Justice Sam Alito or Justice Clarence Thomas) might choose to retire before the end of the year so that President Trump could name a replacement while there is still a Republican majority in the Senate. But that is all it is: Speculation.

I have previously predicted that neither Justice Alito nor Justice Thomas would retire during this presidential term (let alone this year). I adhere to this view.

Today, the New York Times and Bloomberg each report that Justice Alito has reaffirmed that he is not planning to retire this year, and that this week's election results have not altered his intentions.

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. has told people close to him that he does not intend to retire immediately from the Supreme Court, despite Democrats' commanding win in Senate contests on Tuesday, which means Republicans will hold the chamber for only a short time longer.

As a result, Republicans may have missed the window for President Trump to name a fourth or even a fifth justice to the Supreme Court in the final two years of his presidency.

Justice Alito shared his plans with friends after the election results were clear this week, according to two people close to the justice who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The 76-year-old Alito, an anchor of the court's conservative wing, has been the subject of speculation that he might abruptly step down to let President Donald Trump fill the vacancy before Republicans relinquish control of the Senate in January. Such a move could extend Trump's imprint on the court by letting him add a younger, conservative jurist to serve for decades.

The chatter has continued even though Alito said in an interview with Bloomberg News in late September that he had decided to remain no matter how the election turned out. "I intend to stick around through this term," he said then, referring to the nine-month court session that runs through June. "I made that decision many months ago."

Alito indicated that stance hasn't changed despite the Democratic takeover in Tuesday's election, said the person, who asked not to be identified discussing a private conversation with the justice on Wednesday.

While there is no equivalent report on Justice Thomas, there is little reason to think he is going anywhere. Justice Thomas is on the verge of becoming the longest serving justice in the nation's history. Moreover, Justice Thomas has previously said he intends to spend at least 43 years on the Court. Were he to stick to that plan, he would have several more years to go.

While there may not be a Supreme Court nomination to keep the Senate busy during the lame-duck period, there are lower court nominations to consider, including nominees for the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the Fifth, Eighth, and Tenth Circuits. As Michael Fragoso notes in the Wall Street Journal, the lame duck may be Republicans' last opportunity to confirm conservative constitutionalist judges for some time.

Republican senators can make a difference and send a message by putting the Constitution first and confirming the originalist nominees now pending. Petty or parochial squabbles with Mr. Trump may get favorable headlines today but they will be forgotten in a week. A judicial appointment can last a lifetime.

#7610. "The Time, the Opportunity, and the Need to Reclaim the Republican Party from Trump and Trumpism"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I thought I'd pass along this smart and readable analysis from Bill Otis (Ringside at the Reckoning); as I've mentioned before, he and his coauthor Paul Mirengoff are my go-to people for hardheaded, pragmatic, but principled conservative views. They are probably on balance more conservative than I am, but I always much enjoy their legal and political commentary. An excerpt:

In an election where overwhelmingly the preeminent issue was affordability — in other and more candid words, the increasingly obvious decline in the standard of living huge numbers of people are feeling — what has Trump been occupying himself with? Here's a partial list: Building the White House ballroom (from which, in a tone deaf rendition that defies description) he gave his election post-mortem; re-doing the East Potomac Golf Course to make it a "premium" experience; building a Triumphal Arch no one asked for or thought about when they elected him; demanding prosecutions for imaginary vandalism at the Reflecting Pool; invading Greenland; making Canada the 51st state; re-naming Lake Ontario; re-naming the Gulf of Mexico; and perhaps most prominently, making sure his name gets put on the Kennedy Center even though he had nothing to do with its creation. Then there are numerous other items: Trump passports, Trump one-dollar gold coins, and "commemorative" $100 bills, to name three.

Exactly what does this Adventure in Narcissism seem like to the voter — actually, the millions of voters — who feel like they're being stretched thin? You don't need a florid imagination to answer that one. They gave their answer last night.

It's not like Trump has had no successes. He's made three excellent Supreme Court appointments. He has tackled corrosive and unjust racial preferences like no one else had the guts to. He declines to bow to transgender bullying. Objective economic data show that, whatever "feelings" may be, the economy grew at a healthy clip just this last quarter. He used force with Iran when, for nearly 50 years before him, Presidents were content to kick the can down the road as the mullahs got closer and closer to getting the atomic bomb.

These are considerable and important achievements, not less so because Trump often acts like an oaf. But his character flaws throw a wrench into nearly everything he does. It's less that he's an oaf than that he's a child, far too often content to do what's quick and easy while leaving to adults what's messy and hard. The catch is: He's supposed to be the adult. The main thing behind the failures that got Trump his butt-kicking last night is not his classlessness, his carefree attitude [toward] the truth or his gargantuan self-absorption.

The whole thing, as usual, is much worth reading.

Heather Wilson (center), the president of the University of Texas at El Paso, speaks at a news conference announcing that the University of Texas at El Paso will soon launch a law school after the Woody and Gayle Hunt Family Foundation pledged a $5 million matching grant. (Photo from the University of Texas at El Paso’s Oct. 28 press release)

The University of Texas at El Paso inched closer to launching a law school after the Woody and Gayle Hunt Family Foundation pledged a $5 million matching grant.

The school’s leaders aim to present the vision for the law school to the Texas legislature in 2027, with the goal of opening in 2030.

In October 2025, the Paul L. Foster Family Foundation also announced a $5 million matching grant, and El Paso, Texas, law firm Tawney, Acosta & Chaparro committed to a $5 million gift in April. Other El Paso firms—including Farah Law, Flores Mendez Law, ScottHulse Attorneys at Law, and Dallas-based Kastl Law—have made donations that will be matched by the Woody and Gayle Hunt Family Foundation’s grant.

The law school would focus on public and private international law involving the United States and Mexico and aims to address the shortage of fluent bilingual lawyers.

#7607. Karin Slaughter on Mo Hayder, thrillers by women, and the legacy of “Gone”

I clearly remember the first time I read Mo Hayder. Birdman was published in 2000, a year before my own first novel was published, and I felt an intense sense of wonder with every finely crafted sentence. The plotting was fantastic. The characters were not just believable but brought out an array of emotions from lust to disappointment to love to abject fear. The tension knotted more tightly with every turn of the page. I had never read anything like it—and it made me feel more inspired, more challenged, in my own career.

At the time, the genre was a hard place for women. We are supposed to be sugar and spice, the docile victims of these sorts of stories, not the ones who gain control and agency by writing about them with an unblinking eye. That Mo was able to accomplish this, that she broke ground for the many who came behind her, will always be an enduring part of her legacy.

The women who were able to follow, from Gillian Flynn to Ivy Pochoda to Jennifer Hillier, owe a tremendous debt to Mo for helping carve out space in a genre that often celebrates women on the page, but seldom celebrates them the same way in life.

But that’s exactly who Mo Hayder was: a mold-breaker. She was an iconoclast who could not be put in a box, neither as a person nor as a writer. She was bold. Her wit razor sharp. Her humor quirky. She didn’t shy away from writing about very dark things, and that made her an outlier. Her voice on the page was always confident and assured but never bordered into authorial intrusions. She never wrote the same book or told stories the same way twice. Mo Hayder was an icon.

In Birdman, Jack Caffery is a young, driven, seemingly unshockable detective who is faced with the daunting task of hunting down a serial killer who’s leaving behind a trail of horrific crimes—but the story is much more than the plot. Caffery is a character who grabs you by your bones and shakes you into seeing all the darkness in the world. He has messy relationships. He screws up a lot.

But in the end, you’re rooting for him—not just because you want the crime solved but because you want something, anything, to finally go his way. Readers often take it for granted that they will care about a character, but making them care about a character who does unlikable things is the difference between a writer and a master storyteller. Mo certainly deserves that title.

Gone is the fifth book in the Jack Caffery series but it stands very well on its own. By this point, Caffery’s counterpoint, Police Diver & Sergeant Phoebe “Flea” Marley, has been introduced. Marley is a lot like Mo: determined, beautiful, incredibly capable, but not invincible.

Flea and Caffery should have a closer relationship. They would fit together like two puzzle pieces. Unfortunately, they both carry around an awful lot of baggage. While this is tough for them, it makes them come alive on the page. They are excellent counterparts as detectives, and by the end of this novel you’ll be rooting for them both, despite their very deep flaws.

It’s no surprise that Mo won the Edgar® Award for Gone. She takes what already worked so well in this series and pushes up the volume by a thousand. The villain is completely fresh and extremely frightening. The plot takes amazingly satisfying twists that you’ll never see coming. And the story will creep and crawl right under your skin where it will stay forever.

Mo Hayder’s novels are dark, visceral, bold, and brilliant, and she leaves behind a lasting legacy. When she passed away in 2021, the crime writing world was devastated—tributes poured in and readers found solace in her novels—the incredible, brave, important stories she left behind.

Mo was always a writer—and a person—who looked at life as a question to be answered, as shown by her varied career path—not one to simply sit down to write in a vacuum, she made sure she had a wealth of life experience under her belt (she worked as a barmaid, security guard, filmmaker, hostess in a Tokyo club, educational administrator, and a teacher of English as a foreign language, to name but a few). Mo also held an MA in film from The American University in Washington, DC, and an MA in Creative Writing from Bath Spa University.

Writing was her love and her craft, and she took it very seriously. The legacy she leaves behind is not only that of a thriller writer, but of a generous, smart, passionate author and champion of other authors. I remember her as someone who squeezed every ounce out of life and did us all the great kindness of pouring some of that energy into her novels.

Over her many years as a writer, Mo, whose real name is Clare Dunkel, and detective Jack Caffery earned a legion of loyal fans, with Mo’s compulsive stories becoming staples of every crime reader’s bookshelf up and down the country—and indeed, across the globe. The series went from strength to strength, and Mo’s unique writing style and her refusal to shy away from the darker side of life became more and more apparent, setting her apart from other thriller writers and making it impossible for anyone to replicate her.

I am to this day still in awe of her tremendous talent and am deeply saddened that she is gone. We are so lucky that her work lives on.

#7606. Justice Department Announces Results from Operation Not Forgotten 2026

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice and FBI announced today results of the personnel surge in support of Operation Not Forgotten 2026, which focuses on unresolved cases in Indian country with a priority on cases involving violence against women and children, including those who are missing or murdered.

In its fourth year, Operation Not Forgotten surged personnel and investigative resources across the country from April 1 through September 30, resulting in 118 arrests, 41 individuals charged federally, 25 child victims identified or located, and 72 weapons recovered.  FBI agents conducted 990 interviews and 232 search operations.  Arrests increased by 123% and subjects charged by 52% over 2025.

“The Department of Justice will always work to deliver justice for the victims of violent crime in Indian country,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Thanks to the hard work of the FBI, our U.S. Attorneys, and other federal and tribal partners, Operation Not Forgotten and Operation Steadfast Promise are helping make communities safer and providing comfort for victims and families.”

“This year’s Operation Not Forgotten continued this FBI’s largest commitment to Indian Country in the history of the Bureau,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “The results were outstanding – from April 1 through September 30, this FBI worked more than 500 cases, a 59% increase from last year’s operation; 118 arrests, a 123% increase; and 41 subjects charged federally, a 52% increase. This is in addition to 25 child victims identified or located and 72 weapons recovered. These involved life-saving operations, with cases including child sexual abuse, physical assault and abuse, domestic violence, CSAM cases, and more.

“Operation Not Forgotten sends a loud and clear message that our long-forgotten partners in Indian Country are forgotten no more,” said Director Patel. “When I assumed the position of FBI Director a year and a half ago, this FBI promised we would be there for our tribal partners. We have and will continue to be – through our 400 agents dedicated to Indian country, 30 Safe Trails Task Forces, and increased awareness with our Voices Not Forgotten program, where the FBI quadrupled the rewards to at least $25,000 for information associated with homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country. Thank you to our federal, state, and local partners who continue to work with us to ensure these unsolved crimes and cases receive the surge in resources they deserve.”

“Operation Not Forgotten demonstrates the Trump Administration’s commitment to protecting tribal communities, strengthening public safety, and ensuring that victims and their families have access to justice,” said Billy Kirkland, Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs, U.S. Department of the Interior. “Through close collaboration across the federal government and in partnership with tribal, state, and local law enforcement, we are bringing additional resources and investigative support to Indian Country to address violent crime, advance unresolved cases, and help families find answers. The Department of the Interior, through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, remains committed to working alongside our partners to deliver meaningful results and build safer communities for generations to come."

Examples of cases charged during this period include:

In the District of Wyoming, the surge resulted in the federal indictment of 18 individuals for an array of violent crimes, and child abuse offenses on the Wind River Indian Reservation, including U.S. v. Jose Benito Ocon: This prosecution arises from an August 2025 incident near Riverton, where the defendant allegedly executed a male passenger with a gunshot to the head inside a moving vehicle before turning the firearm on two female witnesses.  Leveraging the surge’s enhanced investigative assets, a grand jury returned an indictment charging the defendant with five felony counts, including first-degree murder, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, and two distinct counts of assault with a dangerous weapon. He faces a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment if convicted.  In U.S. v. Darlynn Sheree Seminole, federal prosecutors filed charges following a June 2026 domestic violence intervention by the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Wind River Police Department, involving allegations of severe physical trauma inflicted on a 10-year-old.

In the District of Nevada, in July a federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging Delshay Astor with the alleged murder of Anna Scott, a member of the Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribe, on the Reno-Sparks Indian Colony in February 2022, and also charged Joel Christy for assisting Astor to avoid apprehension.

In the District of Minnesota, Operation Not Forgotten has resulted in four cases charged during the surge period with violent and sexual offenses in Indian Country, including sexual abuse of minors, domestic assault causing substantial bodily injury, assault by strangulation, and assault with intent to commit kidnapping. One recent case includes U.S. v. Courtney John Barrett Sr. indicted on September 22, 2026, on two counts of sexual abuse of a minor.

In the District of Montana, Michael Plentybuffalo was charged in the death of Shann Nomee, who went missing during an extreme cold snap in January 2024 and whose frozen body was found in a field north of Lodge Grass, Montana after a community led search and a tip to the Bureau of Indian Affairs that pointed to Plentybuffalo.  His case is pending trial.

Also in Montana, Lance Crookedarm was charged with the May 2026 violent assault and non-fatal strangulation of a female victim.

In the District of Arizona, at least four cases were charged including two violent assaults, an arson, and the aggravated sexual abuse of a minor under 12, all of which occurred on the Navajo Nation, as well as an additional assault that was committed on the Fort Apache Indian Reservation.

Operation Steadfast Promise, first announced in 2026, is a continuing comprehensive surge of resources to address a wide range of violent criminal threats impacting Indian country. Operation Steadfast Promise builds on the successes of Operation Not Forgotten with the addition of multiple new initiatives to improve public safety in Tribal communities. The FBI, in coordination with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices, the Bureau of Indian Affairs Missing and Murdered Unit, Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and Tribal and other federal law enforcement partners, is working across multiple territories to bring investigative aid to cases and resolution for victims and their families. Since Operation Steadfast Promise began in April, the FBI opened over 1,200 new investigations in Indian country, obtained criminal charges on 678 subjects, made over 700 arrests, recovered 2,260 weapons, and made 140 drug seizures.

This year, Operation Not Forgotten continued to address the over 4,000 open investigations in Indian country including death investigations, child abuse cases, domestic violence, and adult sexual abuse investigations, underscoring the persistent and urgent need for sustained resource investment in these communities.

During Operation Not Forgotten, the FBI surged personnel, including investigative, intelligence, and other support personnel, on rotating temporary duty assignments across Indian country in twelve FBI field offices, in Albuquerque, Billings, Detroit, Denver, Jackson, Las Vegas, Minneapolis, Oklahoma City, Omaha, Portland, Phoenix and Salt Lake City. Working in close coordination with Tribal law enforcement agencies, the BIA Missing and Murdered Unit, and U.S. Attorneys' Offices, together law enforcement worked to advance open investigations and pursue accountability for victims and their families.

Additionally, the FBI has brought focus to a new FBI’s Voices Not Forgotten webpage that includes a searchable and interactive map that brings attention to FBI investigations in Indian country where the FBI, in coordination with state, local and Tribal law enforcement are seeking the public’s assistance. In August 2026, the FBI announced the establishment of a new protocol which created a minimum reward of up to $25,000 for all publicly advertised cases involving homicides, kidnappings and missing persons in Indian country where the FBI has assumed jurisdiction.

The FBI remains committed to standing alongside Tribal communities, federal partners, and local law enforcement to address the violent crime threats that continue to impact Indian country. To learn more, visit www.fbi.gov/investigate/violent-crime/indian-country-crime.

The FBI encourages anyone with information related to unresolved violent crimes in Indian country to contact their local FBI field office or submit a tip at https://tips.fbi.gov.

#7604. Judge advances McDonald’s McRib lawsuit that alleges deceptive marketing

A federal judge in Illinois on Friday did not dismiss a proposed class action lawsuit accusing McDonald’s McRib of misleading customers about the sandwich’s ingredients. (Photo from Getty Images)

A federal judge in Illinois on Friday did not dismiss a proposed class action lawsuit accusing McDonald’s McRib of misleading customers about the sandwich’s ingredients.

The plaintiffs allege that the McRib, which costs $7, is shaped to look like ribs and misleads customers in ads to think that it contains rib meat instead of cheaper pork cuts.

In Chicago, U.S. District Judge April Perry of the Northern District of Illinois dismissed some claims, but she did not accept the McDonald’s argument that a reasonable customer could expect the McRib to contain rib meat. Perry said ads of the rib-shaped patties could possibly be an attempt to defraud, but more proof was needed, according to coverage by Reuters.

“Plaintiffs’ proffered understanding of ‘McRib’ is not unreasonable or fanciful,” Perry wrote.

McDonald’s contends that it does not use hearts, tripe or stomach as McRib ingredients, which the suit alleges. The fast-food giant, which has sold the sandwich since 1981, said distinctive product names do not fool reasonable consumers.

“This lawsuit distorts the facts, and ⁠the claims are meritless,” McDonald’s said in a statement.

#7603. How Alain Delon Got Caught Up in a Murder Investigation at the Height of His Fame

The actor lies still. Eyes closed. Waiting for the signal.

‘Silence sur le plateau . . .!’ shouts director Jacques Deray.

The crew falls quiet. A silence descends upon the Saint-Tropez villa. Just the clicking of the cicadas, drunk on the late-summer heat in the scrubland surrounding the azure pool. Thick cables everywhere. Lighting rigs. Flight cases.

‘. . . Moteur . . . Ça tourne . . .’ calls the assistant director.

The camera motors fire up, a soft clicking as the film turning on the reels gets up to speed. The entire crew poised, ready . . .

The camera pans slowly across the glimmering, phosphorescent surface of the swimming pool until, languidly, it finds him: bronzed, lean, 33. Reclined by the water. Dark hair resting on hot sandstone slabs. A glass of orange juice perched on his belly, rising and falling with his breath.

His other hand toys with the water’s surface. Delicately it is withdrawn. Glistening droplets run the length of his fingers and drip sensuously onto his face, revealing to the camera for the first time one of the most famous men in the world.

Not Narcissus, but something colder, l’homme fatal. Nonchalantly, from being mesmerized by the water’s surface and his own reflection, he turns his head towards the sky, raises the glass from his chest and pours the juice into his mouth, slow and sensual.

Dark glasses on. Eyes closed. Pinned to the tiles by the late-summer heat. The remnants of the orange juice drying on his tanned skin.

He is, for now, untouchable. At the height of his powers.

Once the initial observations are complete, the two forensic pathologists begin the next phase of the autopsy. They make a clean incision across the scalp and peel the skin down on either side, revealing the smashed cranium beneath. The top of the skull is sawn off, the brain removed. Next, they open the torso, slicing through the abdomen to extract the vital organs. No major anomalies, except the liver. Enlarged, discoloured. Consistent with long-term alcohol abuse.

Once the examination is complete, the organs, including the brain, are placed back in the body cavity. The skull is reassembled; the skin pulled back into place and stitched at the crown. Fingerprints are taken and sent to the central police archives in Paris. The man still has no name.

Based on decomposition, the doctors estimate the time of death to be a week earlier, most likely during the night of 22 to 23 September. In their report, they write plainly: the skull had ‘completely collapsed in’. Cause of death: blunt force trauma to the head with a heavy object. The theory holds – for now – that it was a fight, something that got out of hand.

They sign the paperwork. The report is dispatched to the investigating judge.

Patard reads the autopsy report and gives the photographs a cursory glance. He can’t place it, but something feels off.

It’s the hands that catch his eye. Everyone insists the victim is a vagabond. But how many vagabonds have manicured nails?

The next day, a fingerprint match comes through. The deceased is one Stevan Markovic. Thirty-one years old. Born in Belgrade, 1937. The same prints first appear on records in 1958, when this man applied for political asylum in Paris. Then again:

Prison in Chambéry, 1962 La Santé, Paris, 1965 Namur, Belgium, 1964 Annecy, 1967

His last registered address? 22 Avenue de Messine, in the prestigious 8th arrondissement on the Rive Droite. A stone’s throw and the quartier of the Elysée Palace.

Then another twist. When cross-referenced, it would appear that 22 Avenue de Messine is also home to a famous actor: Alain Delon.

A file arrives from the Brigade Mondaine – the Paris vice squad. Technically tasked with investigating moral crimes, the Mondaine is unofficially tasked with monitoring the rich.

Patard flicks through their dossier on Delon, it’s only a few pages long; a couple of minor run-ins with the law. But then there are the photos: Delon with known gangsters, Corsicans, men who once fought for the Resistance and now run rackets out of Pigalle or control the ports in Marseille.

Who exactly is this Delon? Patard wonders. He calls in two detectives. ‘Go to Avenue de Messine,’ he says. ‘Interview Delon. Find out who this man was to him.’

The detectives stand there, open-mouthed.

‘Right,’ Patard says. ‘Let me know what you find.’

Patard glances at the paperwork again. The residency permit lists the dead man as a political refugee. Occupation: doublure – a stand-in. A stand-in, it would seem, for Alain Delon.

Unlike the two detectives, Patard isn’t impressed. He’s never seen a Delon film. Doesn’t plan to. But something tells him – this case is about to get complicated.

Edward Chisholm, author of A Waiter in Paris, was born in England and moved to Paris after graduating from the School of Oriental and African Studies in London. His work has appeared in The New York Times, The Guardian, and The Financial Times magazine. He lives in England.

#7602. Lawprof's First Amendment Case Against Univ. of Kentucky, and a Case's "Journey so Circuitous it Would Make a Baggins Blush"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Benjamin Beaton Tuesday in Woodcock v. Capilouto (W.D. Ky.):

Ramsi Woodcock, a tenured University of Kentucky law professor, has been under investigation for more than a year for controversial comments regarding Israel and Palestine. The alleged comments varied in both content and forum: an online petition calling for the invasion of Israel, listserv blasts to the University faculty and broader legal academy accusing Israel of genocide, the interjection of far-afield remarks about colonization at an antitrust panel in Hong Kong, shouts of "Free Palestine!" while driving two law students near campus, and more.

None of the remarks came in the classroom and none appears to have disrupted school activities. Yet all related in some manner to his role as a state-employed professor—rendering all the more curious the University's July 2025 decisions to promote him to full professor one week and call him in for questioning (literally) the next. {Curiouser still, Woodcock maintains that the remarks in question dated as far back as February 2024 and were known (at least in part) to the University since March 2024.}

The following week brought a public denunciation from the University's President, the start of a formal investigation into potential harassment under Title VI, reassignment from teaching duties to "professional development," and a (since rescinded) ban from campus. {This first of two "Notice[s] of Investigation" laid out four allegations that Woodcock "may have violated" the University's code of conduct and other policies. The notice declared (without elaboration) that the "investigation … is consistent with the First Amendment" and "addresses requirements under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act." A second notice, based on reports from four students, identified four additional allegations that may have "created a hostile environment on the basis of race, color, or national origin."}

Rather than participate in the investigation, however, Woodcock filed this [federal] lawsuit …. The pleadings characterize his treatment by leaders of the University and its law school as retaliation for protected academic or personal speech, violations of the Due Process and Establishment Clauses, and racial and religious discrimination…. The issue ripe for resolution today is Woodcock's request for temporary emergency relief halting the investigation and reinstating his teaching duties.

This is Woodcock's second or third such request, depending on how one counts. And it follows a journey so circuitous it would make a Baggins blush.

The judge previously assigned to this case held a preliminary-injunction hearing in December 2025. Instead of granting or denying interim equitable relief, however, that judge decided to abstain [under Younger v. Harris] on the ground that the University investigation should precede any federal adjudication. The Sixth Circuit, in the spring and summer of 2026, declined to issue a stay, reversed on appeal, and declined to accelerate the mandate. {See Woodcock v. University of Kentucky (6th Cir. 2026) (Because the "the disciplinary proceedings against Woodcock remain[ed] in a preliminary, investigatory stage," the proceedings were not "ongoing," rendering Younger abstention inapplicable). Concurring with the denial of Woodcock's request to immediately issue the mandate, Judge Gilman wrote that "the panel's opinion" did not "in any way limi[t] the sound discretion of the district court regarding how to proceed on remand," but instead "simply h[eld] that the district court erred in declining to accept jurisdiction based on Younger" without "purport[ing] to dictate what should happen upon remand; i.e., whether the district court should immediately proceed with a ruling on Woodcock's preliminary-injunction motion, or whether it should first consider the University's motion to dismiss, or whether it should stay proceedings to allow for the University to complete its investigation."}

Woodcock, meanwhile, filed a parallel lawsuit and TRO request in state court in September 2026—relief that the Franklin (County) Circuit Judge denied without prejudice. {The Franklin Circuit Court consolidated the new case's request a TRO with the First Amendment suit Woodcock originally filed in federal court seeking to prevent former-Judge Van Tatenhove from assuming his role as dean of the UK Law School. After this Court denied his requests for emergency relief, Woodcock voluntarily dismissed the federal claims and refiled in state court.} The Sixth Circuit then remanded and reassigned this federal case to a judge outside the Eastern District after one of that court's [judges] was appointed dean of the law school. Woodcock had previously filed still another lawsuit—also reassigned here, and also to eventually land in state court—seeking to block the dean's appointment on First Amendment grounds. The University investigation (led by a private law firm) resumed in September. And this Court held a TRO hearing in October. Although the investigator anticipated that this phase of the investigation would finish by November 2, that date has come and gone.

Such unusual litigation can raise unusual—and unusually tricky—legal questions. This is true here, even though the crux of Woodcock's claim is superficially simple: the University leaders (Defendants here) took adverse action (investigation and reassignment) against him because of his constitutionally protected speech (chiefly, at least on his telling, Woodcock's self-titled "Petition for Military Action Against Israel"). But resolving this question, at least in the context of preliminary equitable relief, raises several others that Supreme Court precedent leaves significantly undertheorized.

None of the answers to these questions are obvious based on the record in this Court or the precedential decisions of others. Whether an investigation into speech and related conduct amounts to unconstitutional retaliation depends on whether the First Amendment protected the underlying speech and whether the state's response would deter a person of "ordinary firmness" from speaking similarly. Protection for the speech, in turn, depends on whether Woodcock spoke in either his personal or his "academic" capacity. And even if one of those carve-outs apply, courts may still ask whether the "employee's interest in speaking on a matter of public concern outweigh[s] the employer's interest 'in promoting the efficiency of the public services it performs through its employees.'" {Courts also consider "whether the statement (a) impairs discipline by superiors or harmony among co-workers, (b) has a detrimental impact on close working relationships for which personal loyalty and confidence are necessary, (c) impedes the performance of the speaker's duties or interferes with the regular operation of the enterprise," or (d) undermines the mission of the employer."} Additionally, the appropriateness of interim equitable relief turns on similarly difficult—even incommensurable—considerations, including the burdens on Woodcock's ongoing political speech (which appears to have continued in forums outside the classroom), the Commonwealth's interest in controlling the taxpayer-subsidized education offered to its citizens and future officers of the court, and the public's interest in open dialogue, effective investigations, and the avoidance of harassment.

Each of these determinations, courts have illustrated time and again, is fact-dependent. And although a previous judge held an evidentiary hearing nearly a year ago, time and events have not stood still. Woodcock has not, at least not yet, shown that the mere fact of an investigation would chill an ordinary speaker (to say nothing of a tenured professor) in these strange circumstances from engaging in speech on public questions inside or outside the classroom. After all, a university has an interest in "determin[ing] for itself on academic grounds who may teach, what may be taught, how it shall be taught, and who may be admitted to study."

Nor has Woodcock yet shown that the idiosyncratic lawprof speech at issue—in listservs, foreign conferences, links from the UK website, carpools, and the like—is necessarily protected, heedless of forum or audience. {For instance, whether institutional IT policies that restrict a professor's use of school email resources amounts to a "prior restraint," is hardly clear given the prevalence of content-neutral time/place/manner restrictions. And whether a professor's off-topic panel remarks amount to an unprotected "shout-down" or instead protected academic speech, for example, likewise casts at least some doubt on Woodcock's argument that this amounts to pure academic or political speech.} To be sure, whether he spoke in his professorial capacity is hotly contested by the parties—and cannot be determined with confidence or specificity at this stage.

Whether reassignment from all teaching duties would deter a speaker in a retaliatory manner is a closer question. This is particularly true because the University has seemingly identified no past or future campus disruption, little risk that Woodcock's speech has or will infect classroom instruction, and any reason why responses other than prior restraint would be unavailable if Woodcock stepped outside the bounds of his role in the future. On the other hand, Woodcock hasn't convincingly identified any aspect of this investigation or reassignment that is vindictive, disproportionately burdensome, or otherwise out of the ordinary.

Such showings are neither obvious nor obviously foreclosed on the current record. Indeed, they are not susceptible to prudent resolution by a distant district judge in the middle of a semester, when interim relief measured in two- or four-week increments [the duration of typical TROs -EV] is highly unlikely to benefit Woodcock in a manner that outweighs the concomitant disruption to the University's orderly governance of academic affairs. Since Woodcock bears the burden of justifying temporary emergency relief, but has not carried it, the Court must deny his TRO request. When in doubt, the Sixth Circuit has reminded us, "[t]he administration of the university rests not with the courts, but with the administrators of the institution.

These are important questions worthy of further evidentiary presentation, however. To that end, the Court will schedule a second preliminary-injunction hearing later this month. The balance between state governance and individual speech can tilt too far in either direction, of course, and investigations cannot last forever. In hopes of limiting any federal judicial intervention to its appropriate role, and with "reluctan[ce] to trench on the prerogatives of state and local educational institutions," therefore, the Court sets a preliminary-injunction hearing for Thursday, November 19 ….

#7599. ‘Judge Stone’ by Viola Davis and James Patterson wins inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Legal Fiction

Viola Davis (left) and James Patterson appeared in New York City in March for a discussion of their book, “Judge Stone,” which was chosen as the winner of the inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Excellence in Legal Fiction. (Photo by Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images)

Judge Stone, by acclaimed actor Viola Davis and prolific author James Patterson, has been chosen as the winner of the inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Excellence in Legal Fiction.

The prize, which is being awarded by the ABA Journal, the University of Miami School of Law and the University of Miami College of Arts & Sciences, was determined by a panel of judges that featured former ABA Presidents Deborah Enix-Ross and Carolyn Lamm, California Court of Appeal Justice Lee Smalley Edmon and Turow himself.

A public poll hosted by the ABA Journal also chose Judge Stone as the favorite for the prize from among the field of three finalists, which also included A Pair of Aces by Marie Benedict and Victoria Christopher Murray, and Grave Danger by James Grippando.

The Turow Prize aims to honor the work that best illuminates the role of lawyers in society and their power to effect meaningful change. It is a successor to the prestigious Harper Lee Prize, which the Journal and the University of Alabama previously awarded to outstanding works of legal fiction, including novels by John Grisham, Michael Connelly and Grippando.

Judge Stone is a legal thriller about a Black woman judge from a small town in Alabama who presides over a controversial case. It is the first collaboration between Davis and Patterson.

Davis is one of a select group of celebrities who are “EGOT” winners for taking home Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony awards. In 2025, she was honored by the Golden Globes with the Cecil B. DeMille Award for “outstanding contributions to the world of entertainment.”

She won an Emmy for TV’s How to Get Away with Murder and has appeared in numerous films, including Academy Award–nominated Doubt, The Help and Fences (for which she received the Oscar). She won two Tonys (for Fences and King Hedley II) and a Grammy for best audiobook, narration and storytelling recording for her memoir, Finding Me. She also took home a Screen Actors Guild Award for her role in Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom.

In his long career, Patterson has created notable characters and series including Alex Cross, the Women’s Murder Club, Jane Smith and Maximum Ride. He’s written true stories about the Kennedys, John Lennon and Tiger Woods, and has coauthored No. 1 bestselling novels with Bill Clinton, Dolly Parton and Michael Crichton. He’s received an Edgar Award, ten Emmy Awards, the Literarian Award from the National Book Foundation and the National Humanities Medal, according to jamespatterson.com.

Named in honor of pioneering attorney and international bestselling author Scott Turow—the “father of the modern legal thriller”—the Turow Prize seeks to unearth compelling works of fiction that illuminate the dynamics of law, the justice system and the human experience.

Turow’s 13 fiction and two nonfiction books, including Presumed Innocent and the current Presumed Guilty, have sold over 30 million copies worldwide and been adapted for film and television.

Davis and Patterson will receive a cash prize and a signed copy of Presumed Innocent at the award ceremony and reception on Nov. 19 hosted by the University of Miami, along with the exclusive right to feature the prestigious Turow Prize logo on their winning book’s cover.

#7598. Bobcats, “Twin Peaks,” deer: What influenced Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes’ new novel

I love and often teach the memoir People Who Led to My Plays by Adrienne Kennedy. In the book, Kennedy lists all the diverse people, objects, works of art, images, songs, and events that shaped her as an artist. The result is a portrait of a singular artist, a time period, and a manual for becoming an artist.

I have borrowed her form here to explore some of my influences.

Many years ago, my parents sent me a video of a female bobcat being released in the woods outside their home in Northern Wisconsin. It was deep winter, the snow several feet high. An acquaintance of theirs had trapped the bobcat to stop it from terrorizing his neighbor’s chickens and he felt my parents’ woods was a safe place to release her. This news alone would have been interesting enough, but the specifics of the video fascinated me.

The bobcat snarled in the cage, her fluffy winter coat standing on edge, looking both surprisingly small and terrifyingly dangerous. Her captor placed a frozen duck carcass on the snow outside the cage, opened the door, and quickly backed away. But the bobcat didn’t move. She stayed in the cage. The door was open, yet she stayed.

That image captivated me and I started building a story and characters around it.

In my twenties, everyone in my friend group loved Twin Peaks. But I hated it. It frightened me, on many levels, and I hated the way Laura Palmer’s dead and aestheticized body was used to create a story around, a story she had no say in. I wanted to examine this trope of the “beautiful dead girl”: to see if I could write about the real danger women and girls face without making them a spectacle, to see if there was a way to give them agency in a culture that took so much from them.

“—But I love/ life/ I get to be/ in it/ From somewhere else/ in the world/ I am living….”

I consumed all seven episodes ravenously and in quick succession, in the days when I could stay up all night watching TV, letting the images soak into my mind in the thin, vulnerable hours of early morning. I loved the misty forests and the character of the deep, dark lake, the isolation and strangeness. Though the story takes place in New Zealand, the setting felt very similar to places I’d known in Wisconsin. And the missing girl takes action, shapes the story, has a life after the crime that incites the series.

I’d heard and read this folktale, of a mysterious woman completely covered in hair who haunts the jungles of the Caribbean. Her backwards feet confuse those who’d try to track her and her name means “so beautiful” despite or in spite of her sometimes-vengeful nature and her unabashed wildness.

When I saw paintings of her by Firelei Baez—her hair intricately painted fur, her body melding with palms and fauna, her backward feet sprouting kitten heels—the ciguapa began haunting me, stalking in and around my novel.

My family, like countless others, has been irrevocably shaped by the opioid crisis. I carried, and still carry, rage against the Sackler family and others whose criminal and greedy actions caused so much pain and suffering. I wanted to punish them. I wanted to indict them. But I write novels and I didn’t want to write a novel about them. Instead, Clear Water was a way of transforming that rage, of telling the stories of the victims and survivors of this crisis.

In Wisconsin, deer are everywhere. They are full of contradictions: both sustenance and a nuisance—carrying disease, eating flowers and vegetables, totaling cars. They can be both prey and cause destruction. They can seem almost tame, yet are dangerous to approach. They are common and graceful. These contradictions became an intricate part of my book—deer acting as both symbols and forces of their own in the narrative.

Stephen Graham Jones has written many fabulous books since Ledfeather in 2008, but I read this novel at a pivotal moment in the writing of Clear Water. The way Jones interweaves different timelines, the way history shapes the present, and the relationships between humans and animals served as a North Star for my own writing.

I listened to her early albums on repeat while writing Clear Water. Her songs look without faltering at the pain of poverty, violence, and loss yet remain so tender, so full of love and hope.

The forests and lakes of Wisconsin are both the setting of Clear Water and forces that shape the story and the characters. Oaks drop acorns that messages could be carved on. Pines are the only green visible for months in the winter. Birch roots hold the land together. Leaves and pinecones and acorns drop into the lakes, dyeing the water a deep brown tinged with orange.

Even shallow water is opaque. Many beings seek refuge there. Anything could hide there.

Gabrielle Lucille Fuentes is the author of The Sleeping World, Clear Water, and Are We Ever Our Own. She has received fellowships from Hedgebrook, Willapa Bay Artists in Residency, Yaddo, the Millay Colony, Lighthouse Works, and the Blue Mountain Center. She holds a BA from Brown University, an MFA from the University of Colorado, Boulder, and a PhD from the University of Georgia. She is an associate professor at the University of Maryland. She lives in Maryland with her family.
