#7555. Court to consider federal inmate’s ability to use habeas to accelerate transfer to a halfway house or home confinement

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In Maxwell v. Dinis, to be argued on Nov. 2, the Supreme Court will address a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement.

By way of background, when the BOP designates a federal inmate spend time in a halfway house or in home confinement, that portion of the sentence is still considered part of the inmate’s term of imprisonment under federal law and, as such, is overseen by the BOP. That said, such a portion of a sentence is formally distinct from, for example, a term of federal supervised release, which begins after the term of imprisonment is completed and is overseen by a probation officer and a federal district court.

The special character of how a federal inmate serves a sentence in a halfway house or home confinement gives rise to the procedural question that the court is considering in Maxwell.

In 2007, William Maxwell conspired with members of the mob-related organized crime group, La Costa Nostra, to take over a Texas-based mortgage-loan company, FirstPlus Financial Group, Inc., and drain it of its assets. Specifically, Maxwell and others threatened the CEO of FirstPlus by saying that they would accuse him of bribery, money laundering, and other offenses, and took more than $14 million from the company, leaving it with less than $2,000 in its accounts. Convicted at trial in 2015 of numerous offenses, Maxwell was sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Maxwell did not have infractions while in prison, was moved to a low-security facility, and sought to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement by participating in programs established by the First Step Act of 2018 under 18 U.S.C. § 3624(g)(1) and (2). Maxwell argued that the BOP failed to count some of these activities and that he was entitled to between 42 and 48 months of time credit that he did not receive. (Even under the BOP’s stricter calculations, according to the government Maxwell is eligible to be transferred to a halfway house on Jan. 22, 2027.)

The district court rejected Maxwell’s habeas petition, reasoning that he had failed to exhaust his administrative remedies. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit affirmed on the alternative ground that the circuit had adopted a bright-line rule that habeas relief under Section 2241 is unavailable unless the inmate’s claim would automatically entitle the inmate to accelerated release. According to the circuit court, since neither Maxwell’s requested relief of being transferred to a halfway house or home confinement “would entitle him to accelerated release,” he could not seek habeas relief.

What makes Maxwell’s situation tricky is that he is not attacking the validity of his conviction or sentence, which is what is contemplated by the federal habeas statute itself. And under the court’s precedent, it is at best unclear that a federal inmate can challenge conditions of his confinement, such as an inmate’s placement in solitary confinement or in a maximum-security facility. When state inmates have brought such claims about the conditions of confinement, the court has said that they must bring those claims in federal court under a civil rights statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1983, not via habeas.

But at least two initial points seem to weigh in Maxwell’s favor. First, in the 2023 case of Jones v. Hendrix, the court said that habeas remains available as a procedural mechanism for a federal prisoner to “challenge ‘the legality of his detention’ without attacking the validity of his sentence.” What Maxwell is trying to do (contest the BOP’s refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement) can plausibly be described as challenging the legality of his detention without challenging the lawfulness of his sentence. Second, and perhaps more importantly, in 1973, the court held in Preiser v. Rodriguez that a state prisoner must use a habeas petition – and not Section 1983 – to challenge the New York Department of Correctional Services’ denial of good-conduct time credits.

Maxwell begins his argument for why Section 2241 is available to him by relying on language tracing back to a concurring opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia. Specifically, in Skinner v. Switzer, the court stated that habeas relief is available for claims seeking to “reduce the prisoner’s level of custody” (quoting Scalia’s concurrence in Wilkinson v. Dotson). Maxwell also draws upon the language in Jones quoted above and the case of Preiser to argue that the situation in Preiser is a close analog to his circumstances and the court’s language in Jones leaves further room for challenges to the legality of an inmate’s detention.

Maxwell also points out that if habeas relief is unavailable, he has no other alternatives. The court has severely limited plaintiffs’ abilities to bring a civil-rights suit under Bivens v. Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents, for example, and a Section 1983 claim is inapplicable to suits against federal officials. The Administrative Procedures Act is also likely inapplicable because of a statute that limits review of the bureau of prisons’ decisions, as is injunctive relief through a suit in equity.

Notably, the government agrees with Maxwell that alternatives to habeas are unavailable. The government also declines to defend the lower court’s rule that habeas relief is limited to claims that automatically entitle the inmate to accelerated release. But the government endorses a narrower approach to when habeas relief is available than Maxwell. According to it, an inmate may seek habeas relief when arguing that his imprisonment has been unlawfully prolonged, a standard that does not require the inmate to show an entitlement to a sentence reduction. At the same time, the government’s standard would not extend to just any challenge to the “level of custody,” such as allowing an inmate’s classification in a maximum-security prison to be cognizable in habeas.

As for Maxwell, the government contends that his claim should be rejected for failure to exhaust all of his administrative remedies, the ground on which the district court dismissed the claim. On the “merits,” although the government says that Maxwell’s claim is of a type that may be brought in habeas, the government argues that, by statute, Congress has barred courts from reviewing the bureau of prisons’ classification of where an inmate “is placed during his term of imprisonment.” In the government’s view, this statute is fatal to Maxwell’s position.

Because the government declined to defend the court of appeals’ rule, the Supreme Court appointed a “friend of the court,” or amicus. The amicus contends that Maxwell’s and the government’s positions both create line-drawing problems. As to Maxwell’s position, the amicus argues that, given the wide continuum of conditions of incarceration that inmates face within the BOP’s system, determining whether a particular change in custody is meaningfully less restrictive would be difficult as a practical matter and require a fact-intensive, prisoner- and facility specific inquiry. As to the government’s position, the amicus argues that it has not offered any recognizable standard for deciding when an inmate’s imprisonment has been unlawfully prolonged.

In an effort to avoid those line-drawing problems, the amicus argues that habeas relief should instead be available in three relevant circumstances: (1) if the inmate’s claim implies that his physical detention must be shortened or terminated; (2) he is entitled to earlier release on bail or parole; or (3) the sentencing court ordered him to serve his sentence in a place it lacked jurisdiction to send him.

It is unclear whether the justices will find the amicus’ proposed circumstances appealing. But the amicus’s sustained attacks on the difficulties in applying Maxwell’s and the government’s position may well attract their interest.

Richard D. Cooke worked for the U.S. Department of Justice for 23 years, first at the Antitrust Division for 5 years and then as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Eastern District of Virginia for 18 years.

#7554. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#7551. Kim Kardashian aims to retake bar exam

Reality TV star Kim Kardashian speaks onstage during the 2020 Winter TCA Tour on Jan. 18, 2020, in Pasadena, California. (Photo by David Livingston/Getty Images)

Reality TV star Kim Kardashian still holds ambitions to become a lawyer and plans to retake the bar exam—someday.

Kardashian, who failed the California bar exam in 2025, said she is “always thinking about the bar” and is “still all in,” she told People on Monday. “I’m going to take my time and wait until the moment is right, when I have some free time to focus on it.”

Kardashian, who plays a lawyer on Hulu’s legal drama All’s Fair, was among the 7,362 candidates who completed the July 2025 administration of the California bar, according to the State Bar of California.

The state’s test is considered one of the most difficult in the country, and only 54.8% passed last year and 48.3% in July, according to the state bar.

Kardashian did not attend law school and does not have an undergraduate degree. She has followed the state’s alternative pathway that allows candidates to take the bar exam by learning the law through apprenticeship and study.

California is one of the few states that allow lawyers to become lawyers by “reading the law.”

The hospital argues the subpoena was issued for the improper purpose of pressuring it to end gender-affirming care.

(CN) â Rhode Island Hospital asked the Fifth Circuit Wednesday to reverse a federal judge’s order requiring it to comply with a Justice Department subpoena seeking extensive information on the hospital’s treatment of transgender youth, including patient records.

The hospital’s attorney, Matthew Fitzgerald, told a three-judge panel that the order â which was entered the same day the government filed its petition â was issued without due process, as the hospital wasn’t given a chance to respond. He also argued the Justice Department lacked a legitimate purpose for investigating the hospital’s provision of gender-affirming care, saying its real goal was to use a burdensome subpoena to pressure the hospital into stopping such treatment since the feds reached settlements with at least six other hospitals requiring them to do just that.

“Imagine a future Department of Justice that is against the AR-15 rifle,” Fitzgerald said. “So they say, ‘We’re going to investigate the manufacturers of this rifle on suspicion of something â aiding and abetting, perhaps, the drug cartels in Mexico. We’re going to send them subpoenas. We’re going to ask for the personnel files of everyone at the company, everyone involved in the manufacture of these guns, the entire files. We’re going to ask for any contact information they have for the buyer of every AR-15 rifle for the last six years.’ And when the gun companies squeal and say it’s unduly burdensome, it’s for an improper purpose, the government says, ‘Well, if you stop manufacturing this rifle, we’ll claim victory and go away.’”

Justice Department attorney John Bailey said the government is lawfully investigating potential violations of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. While it is legal for doctors in Rhode Island to prescribe puberty-blocking drugs and cross-sex hormones for the treatment of gender dysphoria â a use for which they have not been approved by the FDA â it is not legal for drug manufacturers and distributors to promote such off-label use. But U.S. Circuit Judge Irma Ramirez questioned why the government is seeking patient records if it’s targeting drugmakers.

“If you are investigating whether the manufacturers are misbranding the drugs, then why not start with the manufacturers or limit the scope of the subpoena to communications to the hospital or to the doctors about these allegedly misbranded drugs?” the Joe Biden appointee asked. “Why ask for patient files and personnel files?”

Although the hospital is in Rhode Island, the government filed its petition for enforcement in the Fort Worth division of the Northern District of Texas, where the two active federal judges are both deeply conservative.

Bailey told the Fifth Circuit panel that the hospital is producing responsive records, with patient information anonymized, for the Texas federal court to hold privately while the two appeals are resolved.

U.S. Circuit Judges Kyle Duncan and Kurt Engelhardt, both Trump appointees, criticized the hospital for filing a motion to quash in another court after O’Connor ruled. Duncan said the hospital had created a “procedural conundrum” through parallel proceedings, and Engelhardt called its actions a “sharp practice” that potentially raises ethical concerns.

But Fitzgerald said the case in Rhode Island was started by the Child Advocate, and he argued the hospital was justified in joining that challenge to the subpoena because O’Connor’s order was void for lack of due process.

In July 2025, the Trump administration announced it had issued “more than 20 subpoenas” to doctors and clinics that provide gender-affirming care to minors. This followed an executive order from Trump calling for an end to such treatments, which the president described as âthe maiming and sterilizing of a growing number of impressionable young children.â

Numerous federal judges have blocked or limited these subpoenas, but in August a divided three-judge panel of the Ninth Circuit â the only federal appeals court to have ruled on the issue thus far â overturned a federal judge’s order quashing such a subpoena. A George W. Bush appointee and a Donald Trump appointee ruled, over the dissent of a Bill Clinton appointee, that the lower court was wrong in finding the subpoena was issued for an improper purpose. The clinic targeted by that subpoena has sought rehearing by the full appeals court.

#7548. The Supreme Court and what constitutes cruel and unusual punishment

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Earlier this month, the concept of cruel and unusual punishment briefly captured the country’s attention after the state of Tennessee on Sept. 30 tried and failed to execute Christa Pike. Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, survived being injected with two lethal doses of pentobarbital. As she recovered from her injuries, including arm burns, at a Nashville hospital, commentators debated whether it would be cruel and unusual – and therefore unconstitutional – for Tennessee officials to seek to execute Pike again.

This debate drew attention to a range of past Supreme Court rulings on the death penalty, including a case in which the court allowed a second attempt at executing someone who, as a result of a mechanical problem, survived electrocution. However, it also highlighted a number of unresolved issues in this area, including how the constitutional analysis may change if a state is found to have ignored warnings that an execution attempt may go awry.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7547. Ex-prisoner argues liability of US companies over slave labor abroad

The Seventh Circuit asked if the Trafficking Victims Protection Act gave American courts jurisdiction over accusations of forced labor in American manufacturing facilities abroad.

CHICAGO (CN) â A former political prisoner of a Chinese prison maintained Wednesday before a Seventh Circuit panel that a Wisconsin-based company should be held responsible for violations of federal forced labor laws.

The plaintiff accused Milwaukee Tool Corporation in 2024 of cramping him and other prisoners in a grueling manufacturing facility and exploiting them for the production of Milwaukee Tool’s gloves.

The plaintiff’s attorney Jennifer Bennett argued before the three-judge panel that an amendment of the Trafficking Victims Protection Act â a 2000 law enacted to eliminate modern forms of slavery â grants U.S. courts extra-territorial jurisdiction over any offense, civil or criminal.

“That’s for two reasons, each of which is independently sufficient to reverse. First, this lawsuit is a domestic application of the statute,” Bennett, an attorney with San Francisco-based firm Gupta Wessler LLP, said. “Second, even if an American company profiting in the U.S. from its U.S. participation is not a domestic application, the statute applies extraterritorially, whether it is criminally or civilly enforced.”

The plaintiff brought his claims under subsection 1589(b) of the act, which prohibits âknowingly benefit[ing] … from participation in a venture which has engagedâ in forced labor. But a lower court determined that although the statute grants the government extra-territorial jurisdiction, it does not apply when the statute is enforced civilly.

Chief U.S. Circuit Judge Michael Brennan pressed Bennett further on her understanding of the statute.

“Would your reading make the civil remedy reach farther with fewer safeguards than the criminal prosecution that it rests on?” the Donald Trump appointee asked.

“I don’t think so, your honor, because the civil provision directly only applies to the predicates prohibited by the statute, and so the extraterritorial reach of the civil provision would not be greater than any of the predicates that the remedies enforce,” Bennett said.

Milwaukee Tool’s attorney David Horniak maintained that Bennett wrongfully interpreted the extraterritoriality provision of the act to apply not only to criminal prosecutions, but also to civil remedies.

“We are not looking for whether one can squint at the statute and find a way to read it to apply to civil actions,” Horniak, an attorney at Washington-based firm DLA Piper LLP, said. “We are looking for whether Congress gave us clear, unmistakable instruction.”

U.S. Circuit Judge Joshua Kolar raised concerns about comity, given that the Fourth Circuit ruled in favor of the plaintiff in a 2019 case, in which the plaintiff sought relief after she was sexually abused while working as a housekeeper in the U.S. Embassy in Yemen.

“We’re a little bit worried about just letting anyone dabble in international relations, right? So, if you don’t have that rule, how do you account for that?” the Barack Obama appointee asked.

Bennett noted that the extraterritorially provision is not limited to U.S. citizens, it also applies to companies and people that are present in the United States.

“I think this statute makes it very clear that Congress was thinking about international trafficking, the entire statute is about international trafficking. Congress expanded the extraterritorial jurisdiction at the same time,” Bennett said. “It expanded the cause of action to ensure that it applied to every offense under the TVPA, the findings in the statute explicitly say the reason the United States is getting involved in this is because we don’t think foreign countries are doing it good enough job.â©In other words, Congress itself is making that balance.”

Horniak rebuffed Bennett’s characterization of the statute.

“I think this case raises a paradigm example of the kinds of comity concerns that could have motivated Congress not to extend [the statute] extraterritorially,” Horniak said. “While Milwaukee Tool is the defendant, the underlying conduct at issue here is alleged forced labor in Chinese prisons by the Chinese government.”

“Imagine France enacted a similar law enabling former prisoners in the United States to sue in France for alleged violations of French law based on how they were treated in U.S. prisons,” he added.

Alongside Judges Brennan and Kolar, U.S. Circuit Judge Kenneth Ripple, a Ronald Reagan appointee, also sat on the panel Wednesday. The judges did not indicate when they might rule on the matter.

#7545. Court to hear argument in religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Nov. 3 in a challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado, which argue that their exclusion from Colorado’s universal preschool program is a form of religious discrimination in violation of the First Amendment, because Colorado will not provide them with an exemption from rules that would require them to admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

The Catholic preschools say that they “have no objection to Colorado’s decision to allow over 1,000 … preschools to selectively serve the communities they are designed to serve.” Instead, the preschools emphasize, they “simply want the same accommodation extended to them.”

Colorado counters that the Catholic preschools “remain welcome to participate in” the universal preschool program. However, the state writes, if they do, they must be “subject to the same equal-opportunity requirements that apply to all other publicly funded preschools—public and private, secular and religious.”

Under the universal preschool program, families in Colorado can receive up to 15 hours of free preschool per week at participating schools. To be part of the program, preschools must meet state standards in areas such as employee training; they are also required to sign a nondiscrimination agreement, in which they consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.” Colorado does not allow them to refuse to serve LGBTQ families, because it believes such refusals would violate the nondiscrimination agreement.

The plaintiffs in the case are the Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes with preschools (one of which has since closed), and two parents of preschool-aged children. They went to federal court to challenge the state’s policy, arguing that making Catholic preschools’ participation in the universal preschool program contingent on accepting the agreement amounts to unlawful religious discrimination and that the First Amendment requires Colorado to create a religious exemption to allow them to participate in the program.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit ruled for the state. It acknowledged that in a line of decisions, the Supreme Court has held that “when a state offers subsidies for private education, it cannot categorically withhold those funds from religious institutions.” In the 10th Circuit’s view, however, those cases do not apply to the preschools’ challenge because Colorado “did not exclude” religious preschools from the universal preschool program. To the contrary, the court of appeals wrote, it “welcomed and actively solicited their participation” and it is not seeking “to prohibit funds from being used for religious purposes.” “The restrictions imposed by the nondiscrimination requirement universally cover enrollment policies and conduct, but they are not a targeted burden on religious use.”

The court of appeals also rejected the challengers’ contention that the nondiscrimination requirement is unconstitutional because it burdens their right to freely exercise their religious beliefs. In the court’s view, Colorado’s conditions were neutral and generally applied to every preschool, regardless of religion – the kind of government actions, the Supreme Court held in 1990 in Employment Division v. Smith, that normally do not violate the Constitution.

Although a regulation issued by the Colorado Department of Early Childhood contains a series of preferences to facilitate the matching of families to preschools, including a “catchall” preference that allows preschools to request (and the state to grant) a preference not listed in the regulation, the court of appeals said that preference is not the kind of individualized exemption that would render the law not generally applicable, because the preschools are still required to comply with the nondiscrimination requirement.

The court of appeals also rebuffed the challengers’ argument that the nondiscrimination requirement is not generally applicable because the program permits schools to give preferences to low-income families and children with disabilities. As an initial matter, the court of appeals suggested, it was “not persuaded” that such preferences actually are exceptions to the nondiscrimination requirement because they were intended to protect such children and families and do not discriminate against wealthier families or children without disabilities. But in any event, it continued, the nondiscrimination agreement is still generally applicable because the Supreme Court’s cases only prohibit the state from treating religious activity less favorably than comparable secular activity. And the preferences for low-income families and children with disabilities are not comparable, the court of appeals concluded, because – unlike the exemption that the challengers in this case seek – they do not “undermine[] the government’s asserted interest in ensuring equal access to preschools.”

The challengers came to the Supreme Court in November 2025, asking the justices to weigh in – which they agreed in April 2026 to do.

At the Supreme Court, the justices will review two main questions. The first is the scope of the court’s 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, in which the court struck down a Maine law that allowed public funding to be used for private schools, but not for schools that provide religious instruction.

The challengers contend that under Carson, this case should be “an uncomplicated one.” Colorado, the challengers say, “knowingly excluded Catholic preschools solely on account of their religious exercise” – specifically, “their religious practices of ensuring that all enrolling families are supportive of the Catholic Church’s teachings on sex and marriage and of treating enrolled four-year-olds in accordance with their biological sex.” That exclusion, the challengers argue, places a burden on their ability to exercise their religion, in violation of the Constitution.

Colorado counters that Carson “applied the settled principle that government may not target religion for disfavored treatment.” What the preschools are seeking instead, it says, is a “new rule that would trigger strict scrutiny whenever public-benefits conditions incidentally burden religiously motivated conduct.”

The second question before the justices centers on what a challenger has to show to prevail on a claim that a law is not generally applicable for purposes of Smith.

In Tandon v. Newsom, the challengers contend, the Supreme Court made clear that, for purposes of Smith, “[a] law is not generally applicable if it ‘treat[s] any comparable secular activity more favorably than religious exercise’” – a test that the universal preschool program fails. Colorado created the universal-preschool program to ensure equal access for all preschool-aged children, they emphasize. Because the exemptions for low-income families and children with disabilities allow preschools “to provide families with unequal access based on protected characteristics,” the challengers argue, “they undermine Colorado’s asserted interest in equal access ‘in a similar way’ to” the religious accommodation that the challengers seek. Moreover, the challengers add, the program also fails the “general applicability” test under Smith because it gives Colorado discretion, through the preference system, to allow participating preschools “to discriminate in favor of LGBTQ families and other groups,” such as “‘gender-nonconforming children,’ ‘children of color,’ or members of ‘the LGBTQ community.’”

Colorado pushes back, telling the justices that the law creating the universal preschool program “expressly prioritizes specialized services for” children from low-income families and children with disabilities, based on the state’s “longstanding awareness that ensuring equal opportunity for these children often requires providing them with additional support.” But “allowing publicly funded preschools to provide” such services does not “allow any secular conduct that undermines Colorado’s equal-opportunity interests”; therefore, it says, the law is generally applicable for purposes of Smith.

Similarly, Colorado continues, the system of preferences, used to match preschools with families, that are “unrelated to the characteristics protected by the equal-opportunity requirements, by definition, are not exceptions from those requirements.” It is clear, the state stressed, that such preferences can be implemented “only when” they “do not violate the equal-opportunity requirements.”

Correction (Oct. 30 at 11:40 a.m.): A prior version of this article stated that “a participating faith-based preschool may prioritize the enrollment of families that belong to the same faith as that school.”

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

SAN JOSE, Calif. (CN) â A federal judge was concerned Wednesday about a group of music publishersâ claims of infringement against the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, saying the accusation that more than 20,000 works were copied through torrenting needed specific details.

U.S. District Judge Eumi Lee tentatively ruled to deny Anthropicâs motion to dismiss from the bench before hearing oral argument. However, after listening to Anthropic lead counsel Sonal Mehtaâs arguments, she wasnât fully convinced that the music publishers sufficiently pleaded a claim and asked for additional briefings.

âThe heart of the issue is the inadequacy of the allegations,â Mehta told the court. Furthermore, she said, the plaintiffs provided no details into how or why 20,517 works were chosen as examples of infringement in the suit, saying they havenât taken their claims from âpossible to plausible.â

The music publishersâ attorney Nicholas Hailey said they didnât need to prove a fact to make a claim. He insisted the publishers didnât have access to exactly how Anthropic infringed on all the works and didnât need to show how at a motion to dismiss.

âItâs oddly specific, yet oddly not because of the basis,â the Joe Biden appointee said, noting she couldnât go on âinformation and beliefâ alone.

The publishers say they learned of the activity from the landmark 2025 class action against Anthropic by book authors, Bartz v. Anthropic, and therefore could not bring up those claims in the 2024 filing.

Mehta argued the guardrails incorporated with the newer Claude models do not include materials from the pirated libraries, and they should play an important part in showing how Claude is or isnât continuing to output copyrighted material.

Hailey countered that Claude has memorized the materials and can recall them when prompted by a user, and while it isnât like keeping a dataset that Claude can search from, it still constitutes infringement because Claude was trained on the materials.

Additionally at Wednesdayâs hearing, Lee granted a motion to partially dismiss the case with leave to amend against co-defendant Dario Amodei, a co-founder and CEO of Anthropic. Lee said the publishers failed to show how Amodei committed direct infringement by approving the use of pirated materials.

âJust because Amodei didnât click download on his own computer doesnât mean he isnât directly liable,â argued Hailey.

âEvery CEO for any small startup would be liable under the analysis here,â Lee said of the publishersâ arguments.

Amodei may still be on the hook for secondary infringement, which Anthropic has not challenged, Hailey noted.

Both the 2026 and 2024 cases are going through court proceedings with Lee presiding. The judge has not yet issued her decision for summary judgment in the 2024 case.

In January 2025, Lee ordered Anthropic to maintain existing copyright guardrails for Claudeâs input and output and apply them to future models, but didnât broadly stop training on copyrighted lyrics.

Anthropic has been on the legal hook for its AI since it introduced Claude in 2023. In 2025, RedditÂ suedÂ the company over supposedly training Claude on its usersâ data, and in Bartz v. Anthropic, theÂ company settledÂ for $1.5 billion. It was the largest settlement in the history of U.S. copyright cases.

#7542. Judiciary efforts to create rules for AI stalling amid concerns

Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in the courts have been stalled amid concerns over the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled. (Photo by imaginima/Getty Images)

Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in the courts have been stalled amid concerns over the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled.

The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules, which advises the Judicial Conference of the United States, has been developing rules for AI use for several years, but efforts have encountered setbacks and resistance, slowing down the possibility of any new policy.

Attorneys, scholars and judges have criticized proposed evidentiary rules, such as one involving how to handle AI deepfakes, according to a story by Law360.

“Bottom line: I’m not hopeful at this point,” Maura R. Grossman, a professor at the University of Waterloo in Canada whose research has shaped the AI proposals, told Law360.

#7541. Groups ask Supreme Court to leave lower court order in place halting border wall construction in southwestern Texas

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The plaintiffs challenging the Trump administration’s efforts to build a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to leave in place an order by a federal trial judge in El Paso temporarily halting the construction. Eric Glitzenstein, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the justices in a 40-page filing that granting the federal government’s request to lift that order would allow the Trump administration to “immediately resume blasting, bulldozing, road construction, and other border barrier-related construction across one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States.”

The dispute centers on three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws that then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued earlier this year to authorize construction of the border wall in the Big Bend region, including areas in Big Bend National Park. Noem and Mullin relied on a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 that gives the Secretary of Homeland Security the power to “waive all legal requirements” necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border walls and roads. With the waivers, Noem and Mullin determined that additional border barriers are required in the Big Bend area because it “is an area of high illegal entry.”

The plaintiffs in this case – an environmental group, a local landowner, and a group formed to preserve a church – went to federal court to challenge the waivers’ legality. On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone temporarily barred the Department of Homeland Security from continuing construction on the border wall in the Big Bend region “until and unless” the government complies with environmental and other applicable laws.

In a written opinion issued on Oct. 14 to explain her reasoning, Cardone concluded that the challengers were likely to prevail on their claim that under the major questions doctrine – the idea that if Congress intends to give a federal agency the power to make decisions of vast economic or political significance, it must say so explicitly – the DHS secretary did not have the authority to issue the waivers.

As an initial matter, Cardone rejected the government’s contention that she did not have the power to consider the challengers’ claims because they arose from a statute, while IIRIRA only allows federal courts to hear challenges to waiver decisions if they involve the Constitution. The major questions doctrine, she said, is a “constitutional … rule” based on the idea that “courts should expect Congress to speak clearly when it delegates major lawmaking authority to the executive.”

Turning to the question of whether the major questions doctrine barred the waivers, she observed that both the government and the challengers “appear to agree that the waiver of all legal requirements to construct a border wall in the Big Bend Sector is of ‘major economic and political significance.’” The key issue, she continued, is thus whether Congress clearly gave the DHS secretary the power to issue the Big Bend waivers. It did not, she wrote. She emphasized that another provision of IIRIRA authorizes the DHS secretary to “take such actions as may be necessary to install additional physical barriers and roads … in the vicinity of the United States border to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” When that provision is read together with the waiver provision, she said, it means that the DHS secretary can only waive legal requirements for “construction ‘to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry.’”

But the Big Bend region is not, she contended, such an area: although it “comprises over 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border,” it accounts for only a tiny percentage (“between 0.3% and 2.2%”) of all of the people apprehended crossing the border. This means, she said, that “if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire U.S.-Mexico border. If that were the case, Congress could have simply authorized construction ‘to deter illegal crossings.’” The major questions doctrine instructs courts to avoid “interpretations that would render limiting language meaningless,” Cardone concluded.

The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court on Oct. 21, asking the justices to pause Cardone’s order and to grant review and summarily reverse it. First, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued, the district court did not have the power to consider the challengers’ claim based on the major questions doctrine because their complaint specifically alleged that the DHS secretary “lacked ‘clear congressional authorization’ … to issue the waivers” under the IIRIRA – a statutory claim that “Congress denied district courts” the authority “to entertain.” But in any event, Sauer continued, “[e]ven assuming that the Secretary’s waiver authority implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the Secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction.”

In their brief on Thursday, the challengers insisted that the major questions doctrine applied to their claim, stressing that “the decision to waive myriad federal, state, local, and tribal laws across vast geography for the purpose of building border infrastructure, even through national and state parks where border crossings are miniscule, is a truly ‘extraordinary’ assertion of power.” “Whatever authority Congress delegated, it did not clearly authorize the sweeping exercise of power asserted here, and” the government’s “actions therefore amount to a constitutional violation of the major questions doctrine.”

The challengers also argued that DHS will not suffer any permanent harm if the construction is temporarily blocked – one of the factors that courts consider in deciding whether to award temporary relief. To the contrary, they noted, before Cardone issued her order halting construction, “in response to intense local opposition,” DHS “voluntarily paused construction for weeks in vast portions of the project area.”

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

MANHATTAN (CN) â A New York appeals court dismissed a challenge to a new tax on second homes in New York City on Wednesday, handing Mayor Zohran Mamdani a critical victory for a key piece of his populist agenda.

In a six-page ruling, a panel of judges on the New York Supreme Court Appellate Division, Second Department, ruled that a lower Staten Island judge was wrong to give standing to the group of plaintiffs who challenged the rollout of the novel pied-Ã -terre tax, which targets high-value city properties used as secondary homes.

The order comes after a group of homeowners sued the city in August. They claimed the Mamdani administration unfairly placed the burden on them to prove that they shouldnât be targeted by the new surcharge when it sent them notices that they âmay be subjectâ to it. New York Supreme Court Justice Wayne Ozzi agreed â the Staten Island jurist ruled in September that âhomeowners are being substantially harmed and penalized needlesslyâ by this rollout process.

But on Wednesday, the appellate court reached a different conclusion.

âThe mere receipt of the initial determination notices â¦ does not qualify as an injury, in and of itself, as the notice instead serves an informational purpose,â the panel ruled. âBy legal analogy, the receipt of debt collection letters, standing alone, does not rise to the level of an injury-in-fact.â

The homeowners claimed they received these letters despite their New York City homes being their primary residence, and thus not subject to the new surcharge. Ozzi found that receiving these notices forced them to âexpend time and moneyâ to prove thisâsomething he said the city should have done before sending them out.

âAll taxpayers incur time, effort and costs in determining and complying with their various tax obligations, which vary from person to person, entity to entity, and tax bracket to tax bracket, sometimes widely, depending on each taxpayerâs individualized circumstances within the broader federal, state and local tax matrix,â the court found.

The panel also rejected the homeownersâ arguments that they were harmed by the administrationâs mass publication of potentially targeted properties on a city website.

âThe petitioners did not allege for injury purposes that any bad actors have misused the information purveyed by the supplemental roll, or that the publication itself subjected them to any crime, harassment, or defined public ridicule,â the court found.

Justices Phillip Hom, Deborah Dowling, Francesca Connolly and Mark Dillon reversed the ruling.

In response to the order, Mamdani said in a statement on Wednesday that he was âheartenedâ the appeals court ârejected an attempt by the ultrawealthy to avoid paying their fair share.â

âFrom day one, those with the most have attempted to use every legal avenue available to shield their wealth and avoid contributing more to our city,â the mayor said. âBut owning a second home worth over 5 million dollars should come with a responsibility to the city that makes it valuable. The pied-Ã -terre surcharge asks those who can afford luxury second homes to contribute toward the safer streets, cleaner parks and essential public services that every New Yorker deserves.â

Randy Mastro, who is representing the homeowners, said in a statement that they âremain confidentâ in their fight against the tax, despite Wednesdayâs ruling.

âItâs a shame that, after the city admittedly botched the rollout of this surcharge, the court today took the procedural off-ramp of standing to avoid addressing the merits of this case,â he said. âWhat the city has done here is unconscionable â trying to ensnare thousands of people who donât owe this surcharge into having to prove they live in their own homes or else have to pay it.â

The ruling is a major win for Mamdaniâs administration, in which affordability has been the centerpiece, but the fight is far from over.

While this complaint from homeowners targeted only specific elements of the taxâs rollout â not the lawfulness of the surcharge itself â Mamdaniâs administration is also battling two other lawsuits that accuse the pied-Ã -terre tax of being discriminatory.

Co-plaintiffs billionaire casino magnate Steve Wynn and former Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross brought one of those challenges.

According to Mastro, these lawsuits will be the real test.

âTo be clear, though, the ultimate day of reckoning for this âpied-Ã -terreâ surcharge will occur next month when its constitutionality will be decided,â he said. âWe remain confident we will prevail and put an end to this unconstitutional surcharge altogether."

New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed the pied-Ã -terre tax into law in late May as part of the state budget. She said the citywide surcharge, expected to generate at least $500 million annually, would help close the cityâs budget gap and ensure the wealthiest New Yorkers contribute to city services.

The tax applies to second homes valued at at least $5 million and second condos and co-ops valued at more than $1 million.

#7539. Lab-grown meat manufacturers fight to stay on Texas menus

Two startup food manufacturers of cultivated salmon and chicken argue the ban is economic protectionism dressed up as a health pause.

(CN) â Texas and two California startups fought Wednesday before a Fifth Circuit panel over the enforcement of the state’s proposed two-year ban on the sale of lab-grown meat.

A lower court refused to block Senate Bill 261 in January, but California companies Wildtype and UPSIDE Foods argue the ban was enacted to shield the stateâs cattle industry from out-of-state competition and that they are suffering irreparable harm.

âWe have our lost revenue, our lost business opportunities, our lost goodwill and our lost time in the market,â Institute for Justice attorney Marco Vasquez Jr., representing the companies, said.

Wildtype produces cultivated salmon while UPSIDE produces cultivated chicken. Both products are made by growing animal stem cells into edible tissue and have received federal clearance to sell nationwide.

The Texas law prohibits the sale of âcell-cultured proteinâ in the state until Sept. 1, 2027. The companies contend the ban violates the dormant commerce clause and is preempted by the federal Poultry Products Inspection Act.

Vasquez pointed to statements by the billâs sponsor that âthe goal of this bill is to protect our agriculture industry.â

He also noted the lawâs statement of intent describing its purpose as supporting traditional agriculture. Vasquez also argued to the three-judge panel that neutrality is not enough under dormant commerce clause precedent when a lawâs purpose and practical effect is to cut off an entirely out-of-state industry.

But Texas Assistant Solicitor General Douglass Duncan countered that the ban treats in-state and out-of-state companies the same.

âSB 261 is no different from the law in [another] case that this court upheld that banned the sale of horse meat in Texas,â he said. âIt treats all in-state and out-of-state companies the same by way of a blanket ban as the court said there. It therefore cannot be considered economic protectionism.â

The panel pressed both sides on whether the record is developed enough for the appeals court to decide the discrimination question itself or whether it should send the case back to the federal court.

Duncan noted that the CEO of an Austin-based cultivated meat company testified against the bill at legislative hearings.

âIf a statute threatens to put an in-state company out of business, it cannot be discriminatory against out-of-state companies,â he said.

Duncan also argued that cultivated meat companies are not similarly situated to traditional meat producers. He said the products are marketed primarily to consumers who avoid conventional meat for ethical or environmental reasons, and he cited testimony that UPSIDEâs chicken sells for $200 per pound.

âThere is no basis on this record to conclude that these two products or these two different types of entities are similarly situated,â he said.

He also characterized the companiesâ Texas sales as minimal â one restaurant relationship for Wildtype and a single sale to one resident for UPSIDE more than two years ago â and argued that any harm is speculative and outweighed by the stateâs interest in protecting residents from imperfectly understood risks.

The panel questioned the weight of legislative statements about protecting agriculture versus statements about potential long-term health risks of a novel product.

Duncan described the two-year sunset as a reasonable pause to allow further study.

Vasquez responded that Texas had produced no evidence of health risks and that federal regulators had already reviewed the companiesâ safety data.

The panel â which included U.S. Circuit Judges Don R. Willett, Andrew S. Oldham and Cory T. Wilson, all three appointed by Donald Trump â took the case under advisement. The ban remains in effect while the appeal is pending.

#7538. The November argument session begins on Monday

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

It was a relatively quiet week at the court, as the justices – and the SCOTUSblog team – prepared for the November argument session to begin next week. On the interim docket, the court decided one immigration-related dispute and moved closer to being able to decide another.

On Thursday, an environmental group, a local landowner, and a group formed to preserve a church urged the Supreme Court to deny the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. For more on their filing, see the On Site section below.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court denied a request from three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants to pause an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice that prevents enforcement of a Biden-era rule allowing immigration judges to pause certain deportation proceedings. There were no noted dissents.

The court’s November argument session will begin next week. On Monday, the justices will hear argument in two cases: Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement; and Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

Congress may be “the battleground in the 2026 midterm elections,” but the Supreme Court is playing a role in many races, according to USA Today. Republican and Democratic candidates alike are highlighting “disputes about the high court’s membership, its size and its ethics” and calling on voters to keep these battles in mind when they head to the polls next week. In particular, candidates are raising the possibility of a Supreme Court vacancy during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office and emphasizing that the party that controls the Senate will be able to determine whether another Trump nominee is confirmed to the court.

U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong has “barred immigration agents in Southern California from stopping people based on racial stereotypes,” citing what she described as “a mountain of evidence” showing that agents are “targeting people who appear Latino,” according to the Los Angeles Times. “The injunction … requires agents to establish individualized reasonable suspicion before detaining someone for immigration enforcement.” The Times noted that the evidence cited by Frimpong in her new order “had not yet been turned over by the government when the Supreme Court last year stayed the judge’s earlier order barring stops based solely on race or ethnicity, language, location or employment, either alone or in combination.” Frimpong acknowledged the Supreme Court's decision in her new order, but emphasized that the court “had not explained its reasons for granting the stay.” “This Court cannot be faulted for failing to follow guidance that was never given,” the judge wrote. The Trump administration has indicated that it will appeal Frimpong’s order to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit.

On Wednesday, Utah “filed criminal charges against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, months after a federal judge rejected Kalshi’s effort to prevent Utah from enforcing its strict anti-gambling laws against the activity,” according to the Associated Press. “The charges include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.” The AP noted that “[t]he felony charges could represent a new tactic in how states try to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity, a clash that appears headed to a showdown at the U.S. Supreme Court.”

Last week, the University of North Carolina School of Law “tested whether AI could replicate the reasoning of US Supreme Court justices” by staging “a simulated Supreme Court argument based on an actual case the high court heard in 2025,” according to Reuters. Participants found that although the three AI justices used in the test drew the same conclusions as the real-life justices, “deciding the case the same way the actual court did,” the bots did not excel at mimicking their behaviors during oral argument. “The AI justices asked questions and hypotheticals of the law students who argued the case, but their interactions felt robotic and they didn’t interrupt or interject the way the real justices do.” “There’s still this huge gap in it actually feeling human,” said Nicole Downing, the law school’s assistant dean for AI, to Reuters.

In his newsletter for The New York Times, Adam Liptak explored the Trump administration’s battle against what it describes as “rogue activist judges,” a category that has come to include judges who expressed frustration with government lawyers or criticized the administration’s actions in media interviews. Liptak noted that the Supreme Court held, in a 1994 opinion from Justice Antonin Scalia, that “[e]xpressions of impatience, dissatisfaction, annoyance and even anger” are “within the bounds of what imperfect men and women, even after having been confirmed as federal judges, sometimes display” and do not necessarily establish “bias or partiality.”

The plaintiffs challenging the Trump administration’s efforts to build a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to leave in place an order by a federal trial judge in El Paso temporarily halting the construction.

The court will hear oral argument on Tuesday in a challenge brought by Catholic preschools. The schools argue that their exclusion from Colorado’s universal preschool program is a form of religious discrimination in violation of the First Amendment, because the state will not provide them with an exemption from rules that would require them to admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

(SCOTUSblog Plus) Earlier this month, the concept of cruel and unusual punishment briefly captured the country’s attention after the state of Tennessee on Sept. 30 tried and failed to execute Christa Pike. The botched execution drew attention to a range of past rulings on the death penalty, while also highlighting a number of unresolved issues in this fraught area.

In his Controlling Opinions column on Wednesday, Richard Re reflected on Justice Samuel Alito’s effort in his new book to discourage judicial “insecurity” – that is, “a judge’s self-conscious worry that he might be advancing his own policy preferences under the guise of impartial adjudication.” According to Re, “what Alito labels insecurity is better understood as a form of humility and self-awareness,” impulses that are laudable, not problematic.

As it currently stands, the 2026-27 term is much less Trump-centric than its predecessor. But that could soon change, because by mid-January the justices are likely to consider a number of petitions for review from the Trump administration or Trump himself.

In his Justice, Democracy, and Law column on Tuesday, Edward Foley explored a growing battle over the division of authority between states and the federal government when it comes to “determining who can vote in congressional elections and regulating how the voting process occurs.” One such case involves the issue of alleged noncitizen voting in California, which may soon arrive at the Supreme Court.

In her In Dissent column on Monday, Anastasia Boden explored 1926’s Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty, in which the Supreme Court, after rehearing the case and “a dramatic reversal in several justices’ positions,” paved the way for modern zoning. Boden noted that “[t]hree justices dissented, though they never said why.”

Sarah Isgur and David French zoom in on the cases prosecutors have brought against political enemies of the Trump administration. Then, they review the latest news from the battle over a Washington, D.C., golf course before tackling the administration’s sue-and-settle case in Texas.

The election is upon us, and worries about possible anti-democratic actions have many on alert. Akhil Amar and Andy Lipka peer ahead to see what to watch out for and review the relevant constitutional law and history.

Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice John McKinley, who served on the court from 1838 to 1852.

With the Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act of 1837, Congress added two more seats to the court. The first went to Justice John Catron, and the second went to Justice John McKinley, whose confirmation created a nine-justice court. While the seat itself was an honor, its duties were less so, as McKinley would discover.

McKinley was born in May 1780 in Culpeper County, Virginia. His family soon moved to Kentucky, where he taught himself law, passed the bar in 1800, and practiced in both Frankfort and Louisville. After moving to Alabama around 1818, McKinley grew wealthy from land speculation, partnered with Andrew Jackson in the Cypress Land Company, and helped found the city of Florence, Alabama. Jackson himself called McKinley “the most prominent man” in the state.

McKinley entered the Alabama Legislature in 1820, and, after backing Jackson for the presidency (he had previously supported Henry Clay), won a U.S. Senate seat in 1826. In the Senate, McKinley advocated for bankruptcy policies “favorable to small farmers.” However, his vote to override Jackson’s Maysville Road veto (the Maysville Road Bill essentially proposed federal stock purchases for internal improvements, like state roads) raised doubts about his loyalty, and he was not reelected in 1830. After one term in the U.S. House and another in the state legislature, he won a second Senate term in 1836, only to leave the seat within two months due to his Supreme Court appointment.

In 1837, the Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act expanded the court to nine justices, and Jackson’s advisers pushed McKinley for one of the new seats, but Jackson preferred his friend William Smith instead. When Smith declined, the pick then fell to the newly inaugurated President Martin Van Buren, who went with McKinley. Van Buren gave McKinley a recess appointment in April 1837, and the Senate confirmed him by voice vote that September.

After his nomination, McKinley wrote to then-House speaker James Polk that he had “accepted the appointment, although it is certainly the most onerous and laborious of any in the United States.” The new 9th Circuit included Alabama, Arkansas, Mississippi, and eastern Louisiana and required eight circuit terms a year. McKinley told Polk he would travel more than 5,000 miles annually, although McKinley later reported a figure closer to 10,000. The duties also likely ate into his finances (the justices were required to personally pay for their own circuit court duties) and took a toll on his health (he later had a paralyzing stroke on his way to Jackson, Mississippi).

Even before his first term started, McKinley asked Van Buren in person about changing the new 9th Circuit, but the president left the issue out of his next annual State of the Union, upsetting McKinley. Following McKinley’s first full term, the justices disbanded in March 1838 to “confront some 6,000 cases on their cumulative circuit dockets,” according to Steven Brown, who wrote McKinley’s first full-length biography. McKinley’s share from the 9th Circuit alone made up 4,700 of those.

Brown detailed one of the more interesting stories from McKinley’s extensive circuit duties in a 2011 Journal of Supreme Court History article. In April 1839 while holding circuit court in Jackson, a fight spilled into the courtroom and an officer of the court (who had been called “a stupid jackass” by McKinley for not bringing in the court marshal) pulled McKinley’s nose. Newspapers reported that the justice swore never to return to Jackson, and McKinley referenced the “gross personal indignity” in a letter to Van Buren.

In his 1839 State of the Union address, Van Buren told Congress that the circuit’s schedule and distances made it “impossible” for its judge to keep up. McKinley missed much of his circuit duties, along with the entire 1840 term, due to illness. Combined with his failure to hold court in Arkansas for almost five years, states in his circuit felt “neglected,” and the Mississippi Legislature called for McKinley’s impeachment. Congress eventually reorganized the circuits in August 1842, relieving McKinley of Mississippi and Arkansas; beginning in 1843 he rode the reconstituted 5th Circuit, which covered Alabama and Louisiana.

As for McKinley’s actual approach to cases, he was strongly for states’ rights, supporting them “over the authority of the federal government.” During his time on the court, McKinley wrote 19 majority opinions, four dissents, and two concurrences by one count, 22 opinions by another, and 23 by a third, the lowest per-term rate of his era. One of his opinions for the court was in 1845’s Pollard’s Lessee v. Hagan, where he held that new states enter the union on equal footing with the original 13, including ownership of the lands beneath navigable waters. Four years later in the 1849 Passenger Cases, McKinley argued in his concurrence that the federal government, not the states, controlled immigrants arriving from overseas until they became permanent residents of the states.

Increasingly ill after a stroke in 1842, McKinley died in Louisville in July 1852 at age 72, after 14 relatively difficult years on the court. He was replaced by Justice John Archibald Campbell, also from Alabama.

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: "I think we're... I think it's safe."

#7537. Florida child safety suit against Meta moves forward

A state appeals court rejected the social media giantâs request to throw out the case on First Amendment grounds.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (CN) â Meta must face a lawsuit brought by Floridaâs attorney general over child safety concerns, a state appeals court ruled Wednesday.

In its 19-page decision, a three-judge panel of the Second District Court of Appeal declined to dismiss the case and upheld a lower courtâs order, arguing Meta has not yet proved violations of the First Amendment.

âThe challenged order does not come close to infringing on Meta’s First Amendment rights,â wrote Judge Andrea Teves Smith. âThe order did not alter the status quoâit did not place any new restrictions on Meta, it did not grant the attorney general’s request for temporary or permanent injunctive relief regarding Meta’s operations, it did not limit Meta’s speech or expression in any way, nor did it compel Meta to do anything.â

âIn fact, none of Meta’s First Amendment rights have been altered,â continued Smith, a Rick Scott appointee. âAccordingly, we are unpersuaded by the authorities upon which Meta rests its First Amendment argument to support certiorari in this case.â

Judges Suzanne Labrit, a Ron DeSantis appointee, and Robert Morris, a Charlie Crist appointee, concurred.

Florida first filed suit against Meta in 2024, claiming the social media giant misled parents about the dangers of its social media platforms in violation of the stateâs Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

In August, Meta agreed to a landmark settlement with 47 states and Washington, D.C., over claims the company purposely made its apps addictive to children. As part of the settlement, in which the company could pay up to $17.1 billion in civil penalties, Meta agreed to time caps, limits on notifications and restrictions on access between midnight and 6 a.m.

Florida, however, did not join the settlement. Last month, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier renewed demands that Meta mitigate social mediaâs harm to children with a motion for a temporary injunction limiting minorsâ access to Facebook and Instagram. The Republican attorney general chastised Meta for not acting fast enough to remove its youngest Florida users and eliminate certain âaddictive featuresâ such as âlike counts.â Uthmeier also wants the company to limit teensâ screen time on its apps to two hours, end late-night notifications and prevent âinfinite scrolling.â

A Pasco County Circuit Court judge declined to issue the injunction and let the case proceed. Meta responded with a writ of certiorari to the state appellate court, arguing free speech violations and asking for immunity under Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act that limits online platforms from liability for third-party content.

In Wednesdayâs ruling, the appellate judges rejected those claims.

âThis type of limited statutory immunity is not absolute immunity from involvement in any type of lawsuit, such that, here, Meta would suffer irreparable harm merely by litigating the matter,â Smith wrote.

In a post on X, Uthmeier celebrated the decision.

âUnlike other states, Florida isnât going to sell out,â he wrote. âWe will hold Meta accountable for its design features that target and addict our kids.â

A Meta spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but in the past, the company has pointed to new parental supervision controls and time limits for teens.

Floridaâs attorney general has focused heavily on social media companiesâ effects on children, including defending the 2024 state law banning social media accounts for children under 14. In April, Uthmeier filed a lawsuit against Snapchat over violations of that law. Two months later, the attorney general sued TikTok. Last year, he went after Roblox for insufficient age verification controls to prevent children from accessing adult content while also allowing adults to contact minors.

The gun restrictions took effect in Colorado in August, limiting ownership of semiautomatic rifles to those who completed a safety course.

DENVER (CN) â A federal judge on Wednesday denied gunownersâ request to block enforcement of a Colorado law banning rapid-fire devices and restricting ownership of semiautomatic firearms to individuals who passed a safety course.

âThe court concludes that plaintiffs have not demonstrated that they are substantially likely to succeed on the merits of their Second Amendment challenge,â Senior U.S. District Judge William Martinez wrote in a 35-page opinion.

âAccordingly, plaintiffs are unlikely to suffer irreparable injury, which rises and falls here with its likelihood of success on the merits. Finally, the balance of the equities and public interest â Â construed together â tips in favor of defendants,â the Barack Obama appointee added.

Lawmakers passed SB25-3, the âAct Concerning the Prohibition of Certain Semiautomatic Firearms and Rapid-Fire Devices,â in 2025. The law took effect in August with first-time violators being penalized with a class 2 misdemeanor and subsequent infractions rising to a class 6 felony.

In order to purchase a semiautomatic weapon in Colorado, the law now requires individuals to complete a hunter education class with a four-hour safety course, or an extended 12-hour class spanning two days. The class must be taught by a sheriff-verified firearms instructor, with the final exam results recorded in a statewide database.

The sheriff is generally required to issue an eligibility card to anyone who completes the required coursework, but may deny a card if they have âreasonable belief that the documented previous behavior by the applicant makes it likely the applicant will present a danger to themselves or others.â

Aiming to block the law, six individuals and the Colorado State Shooting Association sued Governor Jared Polis and Attorney General Philip Weiser, both Democrats. Weiser won term-limited Polisâ position in Tuesdayâs election.

In addition to citing concerns over the state law handing off implementation to county sheriffs, the gunowners cited the high monetary and temporal cost of complying with the law as burdens that warranted a preliminary injunction.

To make their case, the gunowners pointed Martinez to the 2022 U.S. Supreme Court decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. Under the high court’s two-step test, plaintiffs must first establish their conduct is protected by the Second Amendment, then the government is required to demonstrate its restriction is âconsistent with the principles that underpin our nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.â

Citing the Third Circuit, the gunowners argued semiautomatic rifles are in commonly use and therefore protected by the Second Amendment. The state, however, pointed to decisions in the Fourth and Seventh Circuits concluding âthe AR-15 is a combat rifle that is both ill-suited and disproportionate to self-defense. It thereby lies outside the scope of the Second Amendment.â

The U.S. Supreme Court is expected to settle the circuit split this term. In the meantime, however, Martinez concluded the gunowners failed to show âlaw-abiding citizens commonly use specified semiautomatic firearms today for self-defense.â

âNot only are these semiautomatic firearms particularly devastating to living tissue, not to mention commonly used in mass shootings; but there is also limited evidence to support them being necessary weapons for the self-defense of civilians,â Martinez wrote.

Because the gunowners failed to overcome Bruenâs first step, Martinez did not evaluate whether the state law adequately compared to historical regulations.

The firearm advocates are represented by the Mountain States Legal Foundation in Lakewood, Colorado and First & Fourteenth in D.C. They did not immediately return an inquiry for comment.

The Colorado Attorney Generalâs Office did not immediately respond to an inquiry for comment.

#7535. Lawyers’ AI use doesn’t justify slashing $115K fee award, appellate court says

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award. (Image from Shutterstock)

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award.

Reuters reported Monday that the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver upheld a $115,000 fee awarded to defense lawyers at Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck by the lower court in a trade secrets dispute. The trial court had ruled that the fee was reasonable.

“Plaintiffs have not shown that defense counsel’s use of AI rendered the hours that ​they actually expended unreasonable,” wrote 10th Circuit Judge Carolyn McHugh for a unanimous three-judge panel.

The appeals court also upheld the ​dismissal of the lawsuit.

In her opinion, McHugh acknowledged that AI and similar research tools can make attorneys more efficient. But she stressed that lawyers must still verify legal authorities and arguments themselves.

According to Reuters, the case began in 2024, when industrial motor-efficiency equipment maker Flux Drive filed a suit against a Chinese manufacturer, alleging that one of its former engineers had stolen proprietary information and given it to them. After the case was dismissed, Flux Drive was ordered to pay the defendants’ legal fees. On appeal, the company argued that the defense billed for “ministerial tasks,” and that AI use should have lowered the bill.

The defendants countered that their lawyers checked every piece of AI-assisted research, and that Flux Drive pointed to no specific inflated entry, redundant task or unreasonable charge.

Brownstein Hyatt partner Christopher Ottele, who represented the defendants, called AI a powerful tool that sophisticated firms should embrace.

“This ​decision confirms that the use of AI is not a substitute for the judgment and analysis that attorneys still ​must exercise in every filing with the court,” Ottele told Reuters.

Counsel for the plaintiffs did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.
